title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Purpose of Water Surveillance
Why Continuous Monitoring?
Definition: Systematic monitoring of drinking water to protect public health
Core Objectives: 1. Detect contamination early - Before illness outbreak 2. Verify treatment effectiveness - Ensure purification works 3. Monitor distribution system - Prevent recontamination 4. Track compliance - With drinking water standards 5. Identify emerging threats - New chemicals, antibiotic resistance
Health Impact: - Prevents waterborne disease outbreaks - Protects vulnerable populations - Ensures equitable water access - Provides data for policy decisions

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
The 11-Point Surveillance Framework
Comprehensive Oversight Activities
WHO & Indian Guidelines Recommend:

Approval of new sources (including private-owned supplies)
Watershed protection - Prevent catchment contamination
Construction & operating procedures approval
Sanitary surveys - Inspect water infrastructure
Monitoring programmes - Regular water quality testing
Certification of operators - Trained personnel
Regulation of chemical substances - Used in water treatment
Cross-connection control - Prevent sewage mixing
Back-flow prevention - Stop reverse contamination
Leak detection control - Identify distribution system failures
Codes of practice - Well construction, pump installation, plumbing standards

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 1: Source Approval
Evaluating New Water Sources
Assessment Criteria:
Quantity Assessment: - Safe yield adequate for 95% of year - Account for: Peak demand, seasonal variation, population growth - Design period: 10-50 years future projection
Quality Assessment: - Chemical analysis (heavy metals, salts) - Microbiological testing (coliforms, pathogens) - Physical parameters (turbidity, color) - Comparison with WHO standards
Feasibility Evaluation: - Available at reasonable cost - Treatability: Can be rendered safe economically - Accessibility: Proximity to population served - Sustainability: Long-term viability
Approval Decision: - Only sources meeting ALL criteria approved - Private wells require inspection & approval - Regular re-evaluation for continued suitability

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 2: Watershed Protection
Protecting Source Water Quality
Catchment Area Management: - Area draining into reservoir/water body - Primary protection zone around intake - Prevent human/animal intrusion - Restrict agricultural runoff
Prohibited Activities: - Livestock grazing near source - Human habitation upstream - Waste disposal in catchment - Industrial effluent discharge - Deforestation (increases turbidity)
Implementation Measures: - Boundary marking & fencing - Regular monitoring patrols - Community education - Legal enforcement - Vegetation maintenance
Example: Protected springs require structures preventing direct contamination

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 3: Water Works Procedures
Infrastructure Standards
Disinfection Protocols: - Plant disinfection after construction - Distribution system flushing - Regular chlorination cycles - Documentation of procedures
Routine Maintenance: - Pipe cleaning schedules - Valve inspection & repair - Reservoir cleaning (annually) - Equipment servicing
Emergency Procedures: - Pipeline break response - Contamination incident protocols - Public notification procedures - Alternative supply arrangements - Boil water advisories (when needed)
Documentation: - Maintenance logs - Test results records - Incident reports - Operator certifications

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 4: Sanitary Surveys
Field Inspection Assessment
Structural Inspection: - Source protection adequacy - Pipe integrity (no breaks, leaks) - Storage tank condition (cracks, contamination) - Treatment plant operation efficiency - Distribution network assessment
Risk Identification: - Contamination risks (sewage proximity) - Maintenance deficiencies - Operator competence issues - Treatment gaps - Cross-connection hazards
Rating System: - High risk: Immediate intervention needed - Medium risk: Corrective action plan - Low risk: Routine monitoring - No risk: Maintain standards
Follow-up: - Recommendations documented - Timeline for corrections - Re-inspection after fixes - Training for operators if needed
Frequency: - High-risk systems: Quarterly - Medium-risk: Semi-annual - Low-risk: Annual - Emergency situations: Unscheduled

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 5: Monitoring Programmes
Regular Water Quality Testing
Central Laboratory Services: - Analyze water samples - Equipment maintenance & calibration - Quality assurance protocols - Data management & reporting
Regional Laboratory Network: - Distributed sampling sites - Local analytical capacity - Faster turnaround time - Community access
Sampling Protocol: - Representative sampling (multiple points) - Standardized containers (sterile) - Preservation methods (chilled, chemicals added) - Chain of custody documentation - Aseptic technique (prevents contamination)
Testing Frequency: - High-risk sources: Daily or continuous - Municipal supplies: Weekly - Community systems: Monthly - Small piped systems: Quarterly - Seasonal adjustment for pollution risk

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 6: Operator Certification
Personnel Competence Assurance
Training Requirements: - Basic water treatment principles - Equipment operation & maintenance - Quality testing procedures - Safety protocols - Record keeping - Emergency response
Certification Levels: - Level 1: Small piped/point systems - Level 2: Large community systems - Level 3: Municipal treatment plants - Level 4: Advanced systems with specialized technology
Educational Pathway: - Classroom theory (fundamentals) - Practical training (hands-on) - On-the-job apprenticeship - Examination & certification - Continuing education (annual/biennial)
Monitoring Operators: - Assessment visits - Performance evaluation - Troubleshooting assistance - Refresher training as needed

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 7: Chemical Regulation
Treatment Chemical Management
Substances Used: - Coagulants: Alum, ferric sulfate - Disinfectants: Chlorine, ozone - pH adjustment: Lime, soda ash - Corrosion control: Phosphates, pH buffering - Sequestrants: For hardness control
Quality Standards: - Purity specifications for chemicals - Impurity limits (heavy metals, arsenicals) - Certificate of analysis required - Regular supplier audit
Dosing & Monitoring: - Calibrated equipment mandatory - Regular testing of residuals - Documentation of chemical use - Operator training on safe handling
Safety Requirements: - Proper storage facilities - Personal protective equipment - Emergency response procedures - Waste disposal protocols - Staff training

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 8: Cross-Connection Control
Preventing Backflow Contamination
What is a Cross-Connection? - Unprotected link between potable & non-potable systems - Allows contaminated water to enter drinking supply - Examples: Toilet fill pipes, fire sprinklers, industrial water
Hazards Posed: - Sewage backflow into water supply - Industrial chemicals mixing - Gray water contamination - Pathogenic microorganism introduction
Prevention Measures: - System inspection & mapping - Physical separation (best method) - Air gaps on fixtures - Check valves (one-way only) - Vacuum breakers on hose connections - Backflow prevention assemblies
Regulatory Approach: - Plumbing code requirements - Permits for new connections - Regular audits of high-risk areas - Public education - Penalties for violations

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 9: Leak Detection
Distribution System Integrity
Why Leaks Matter: - Water loss (volume, cost) - Pressure drop (invites contamination) - Ingress of pathogens into pipes - Distribution system vulnerability
Types of Leaks: - Major leaks: Visible (street flooding, puddles) - Minor leaks: Hidden (slight pressure loss) - Service line leaks: Private property - Main line breaks: System-wide impact
Detection Methods: - Acoustic listening devices - Sound of water escaping - Pressure monitoring - Drop indicates break - Flow monitoring - Night-flow analysis (demand low) - Dye tracing - Follows water path - Thermal imaging - Temperature anomalies - Ground-penetrating radar - Subsurface detection
Repair Protocol: - Isolate affected section - Excavate & repair/replace pipe - Pressure testing before reopening - Chlorine flushing post-repair - Microbiological testing - Documentation & record

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 10: Well Construction Standards
Codes of Practice for Groundwater
Site Selection: - At least 15 meters from contamination sources - Higher elevation than potential sources - Accessible for maintenance - Community consultation
Sanitary Well Construction: - Proper lining (brick, cement) to ≥6 meters depth - Parapet wall ≥70-75 cm above ground - Cement concrete platform ≥1 meter radius - Drainage slope outward - Covered top (critical for safety) - Hand pump installation with proper foundation
Deep Well Requirements: - Below first impervious layer - Professional drilling required - Strainer properly installed - Water-tight casing - Maintenance schedule
Abandonment Protocol: - Seal derelict wells to prevent contamination - Prevent standing water (mosquito breeding) - Ground-level capping minimum - Proper decommissioning documentation

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 11: Plumbing Standards
Household Connection Quality
Building Connection Requirements: - Non-corrosive materials (no lead pipes) - Minimum pipe diameter maintained - Proper slope (prevents stagnation) - Isolation valves (for maintenance) - Backflow prevention at connection
In-Home Plumbing: - Separation of drinking water from sewage - No cross-connections to toilets/baths - Proper venting (prevents air locks) - Temperature control (cold water separate) - Regular inspection requirement
Storage Tank Quality: - Sanitary design (sealed, accessible) - Regular cleaning (annually minimum) - Overflow prevention - First-flush exclusion (prevents contamination) - Screening against insects
Inspection & Certification: - Plumbing permits required - Code compliance verification - Pressure testing mandatory - Chlorine flushing post-installation - Microbiological sampling

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Sampling Protocols
Aseptic Collection Techniques
Sample Container Requirements: - Sterile containers (critical for microbiology) - Glass or polycarbonate (not metal) - Sealed caps (tamper-proof) - Labeled with date, time, location - Proper volume (100-250 mL typical)
Collection Procedure: 1. Identify location - Fixed monitoring point 2. Flush line - 30 seconds (removes standing water) 3. Flame tap - Optional (kills surface bacteria) 4. Collect aseptically - Avoid touching inside container 5. Seal immediately - Prevent evaporation 6. Record metadata - Time, temperature, observer 7. Preserve sample - Chilled (4°C) or chemical additive
Transport & Storage: - Deliver within 24 hours - Keep chilled during transport - Avoid exposure to light - Document chain of custody - Note any delays or anomalies
What NOT to Do: - ✗ Do NOT rinse container (removes preservative) - ✗ Do NOT collect from just-cleaned taps - ✗ Do NOT collect in dirty containers - ✗ Do NOT leave sample at room temperature - ✗ Do NOT forget labels/documentation

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Bacteriological Surveillance
Detecting Microbial Contamination
Presumptive Coliform Test (Traditional): - Multiple tube method with lactose broth media - Gas production in tubes = presumptive positive - Confirms presence of coliforms - Limitation: Not specific to fecal origin
Confirmatory Tests: - EMB Agar: Differentiates E. coli (typical appearance) - Gram Staining: Confirms gram-negative rods - Biochemical Tests: Lactose fermentation, indole production - Culture Isolation: Identifies specific species
Membrane Filtration Technique (Modern): - Water filtered through 0.45 μm membrane - Membrane placed on selective media (mFC, mTEC) - Incubated 24 hours at specific temperature - Colonies counted directly - Advantage: Quantitative, faster, economical
Enzyme Substrate Testing (Advanced): - Presence of enzyme-substrate interaction indicates organism - Rapid results (2-4 hours) - Specific for E. coli - Used in developed countries

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Fecal Indicator Organisms
Understanding Test Interpretation
E. coli (Fecal Coliform): - Most specific fecal indicator - Human & animal intestines - Indicates recent/direct contamination - Drinking water standard: Absent (0 CFU/100mL) - If present: System failure, immediate action needed
Fecal Streptococci: - Human & animal origins (distinguishable by species) - More resistant than E. coli - Indicates: Fecal contamination (less recent) - Helps assess contamination age/source - Ratio E. coli:Strep helps determine source
Total Coliforms: - Environmental organisms (some non-fecal) - Include: E. coli + other coliforms - Indicates: Potential for contamination - Drinking water standard: Absent or <5% samples - Less specific than E. coli alone
Clostridium perfringens: - Spore-forming anaerobe - Indicates: Remote/past contamination - More resistant to treatment & disinfection - Used: To assess treatment adequacy - Especially useful for RO/UV system verification

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Colony Count Procedures
Heterotrophic Plate Count (HPC)
Purpose: - General indicator of bacterial load - Non-specific (measures total viable bacteria) - Indicates water quality broadly - Early warning system
Procedure: - Dilute water samples (10⁻¹, 10⁻², etc.) - Plate on nutrient agar media - Incubate 48 hours at 35-37°C - Count colonies (30-300 range optimal) - Calculate CFU/mL
Interpretation: - <1000 CFU/mL: Good water quality - 1000-10,000: Acceptable (investigate source) - >10,000: Indicates problem (contamination or stagnation) - Sudden increase: Potential breach in system
Limitations: - Does not identify organisms - Does not distinguish pathogenic from non-pathogenic - Temperature-dependent growth - Some organisms won’t grow on standard media

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Chemical Surveillance Testing
Monitoring Contaminant Levels
Physical Parameters: - Turbidity: Nephelometer (NTU) - Color: Spectrophotometer (TCU) - Conductivity: Electrical conductance (μS/cm) - Temperature: Thermometer (°C) - pH: pH meter (0-14 scale)
Inorganic Chemicals: - Heavy metals: Atomic absorption spectrophotometry (AAS) - Ions (chloride, fluoride, nitrate): Ion chromatography - Hardness: EDTA titration - Iron/manganese: Colorimetric methods
Disinfection Residuals: - Chlorine (free & total): DPD method (diethyl-p-phenylenediamine) - Ozone: Specific analyzer - UV dosage: Radiometer measurement
Organic Compounds: - Pesticides: Gas chromatography (GC) - PAH: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) - Volatile organics: GC-mass spectrometry

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Quality Testing Standards
Drinking Water Compliance
WHO Drinking Water Quality Guidelines:
Physical Standards: - Turbidity: <1 NTU (or <5 for systems without continuous monitoring) - Color: <5 TCU - Taste/Odor: Absent
Microbiological Standards: - E. coli: Absent (0/100 mL) - Enterococci: Absent (0/100 mL) - Enterovirus: Absent (0/100 L)
Chemical Standards: - Arsenic: 0.01 mg/L (10 μg/L) - Lead: 0.01 mg/L (10 μg/L) - Fluoride: 1.5 mg/L (upper limit) - Nitrate: 50 mg/L - (See Module 6 for complete chemical list)
Monitoring Frequency: - Microbiological: Minimum weekly (high-risk weekly, small systems monthly) - Chemical: Annual (or more if risk identified) - Physical: Daily visual, periodic testing

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Testing Methodology Gaps
Common Challenges
Infrastructure Gaps: - Limited laboratory capacity in remote areas - Expensive equipment maintenance - Shortage of trained technicians - Lack of quality control reagents
Technical Challenges: - Complex matrices interfere with testing - Environmental samples harder than pure cultures - Method validation for local conditions - Equipment calibration drift
Capacity Building Needs: - Training programs inadequate - Continuing education limited - Standardization across regions - Quality assurance protocols weak
Solutions: - Mobile laboratories - Simple field test kits (rapid testing) - Regional central labs (reference standards) - Capacity building partnerships - Digital reporting systems

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Rapid Testing Methods
Field-Level Assessment
Advantages of Rapid Tests: - Results within hours (not days) - Lower cost than laboratory testing - Portable (field deployment) - Minimal training needed - Good for screening purposes
Available Rapid Tests: - Colilert system: Most probable number (MPN) in 18-24 hours - Chromogenic substrates: Color change indicates E. coli - ATP bioluminescence: Organic matter indicator - Conductivity probes: Salinity/TDS quick assessment - Turbidity meters: Handheld devices
Limitations: - Less specific than laboratory methods - Cannot identify organisms definitively - Confirmation testing still needed for positives - Variability in technique
Best Practice: - Use rapid tests for screening - Confirm positive results in laboratory - Regular comparison with reference methods

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Data Management & Reporting
Surveillance Information System
Data Recording: - Date, time, location of sample - Source identification - Test results with units - Analyst name & signature - Quality assurance notes - Corrective actions taken
Database System: - Digital recording (prevent errors) - Backup systems (prevent loss) - Secure access (confidentiality) - Trend analysis capability - Report generation automated
Reporting Structure: - To water authority (daily for major issues) - To public health department (monthly) - To consumers (transparency) - To government (compliance verification) - International reporting (WHO, SDG tracking)
Public Communication: - Water quality report cards (annual) - Boil water notices (when needed) - Violation reports (transparent) - Community meetings - Website/app access to data

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Response Protocol
When Contamination is Detected
Immediate Actions (Within Hours): 1. Verify result: Retest to confirm contamination 2. Identify source: Pinpoint location/cause 3. Assess risk: Determine population affected 4. Notify public: Issue boil water notice if needed 5. Alert authorities: Health department, water authority 6. Begin investigation: Trace contamination source
Short-term Response (24-72 hours): - Increase testing frequency - Check nearby samples (pattern analysis) - Inspect infrastructure (pipes, tanks) - Review treatment plant operation - Interview affected persons (symptom surveillance)
Corrective Actions (Days-Weeks): - Repair identified defects - Optimize treatment - Flushing/disinfection of system - Resampling to confirm resolution - Root cause analysis - Prevention measures
Communication: - Initial notice (contamination detected) - Updates on progress - All-clear notice (contamination resolved) - Post-incident review - Lessons learned documentation

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Early Detection Systems
Advanced Surveillance Technologies
Continuous Monitoring: - On-line turbidity sensors - Chlorine residual monitors - pH continuous recording - Flow rate measurement - Unusual pattern alert systems
Wastewater Epidemiology: - Sewage sampling for pathogen detection - Early indicator of community infection - COVID-19 application (wastewater PCR) - Poliovirus surveillance - Antimicrobial resistance tracking
Syndromic Surveillance: - Hospital admission monitoring (diarrhea cases) - School absenteeism tracking - Emergency department visits - Pharmacy data (antidiarrheal sales) - Pattern recognition for outbreaks
Genomic Surveillance: - DNA sequencing of isolated pathogens - Strain tracking during outbreaks - Source attribution - Resistance mutation identification - Epidemiological investigation

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Case Study: Outbreak Investigation
Scenario - Cholera Detection
Initial Detection: - 15 cases of acute diarrhea in one area within 48 hours - Stool samples positive for V. cholerae - Public health alert triggered
Surveillance Actions: 1. Immediate testing: Water samples from implicated zone 2. Confirmatory testing: Coliform presence (YES - breach!) 3. Source tracing: Pipeline break near sewage line identified 4. Health response: ORS distribution, IV fluids 5. Communication: Boil water notice issued 6. Community measures: Chlorination, flushing begun
Investigation Findings: - Pipeline break at 7-meter mark - Back-pressure from sewage during low-flow period - Sewage contamination entered supply - ~2000 people affected
Corrective Actions: - Pipeline repaired (24 hours) - System flushing & chlorination (48 hours) - Microbiological testing cleared (72 hours) - All-clear issued - Root cause: Maintenance backlog
Prevention: - Pipeline replacement plan initiated - Increased monitoring frequency - Maintenance schedule intensified - Operator training reinforced

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
International Surveillance Coordination
Global Disease Tracking
WHO Surveillance: - International Health Regulations (IHR) - Notifiable diseases include waterborne outbreaks - Data sharing between countries - Coordinated response for pandemics
Regional Networks: - South-East Asia surveillance - Cross-border waterborne disease monitoring - Training & capacity building exchange - Reference laboratory network
India’s Role: - National Waterborne Disease Surveillance System - IDSP (Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme) - State-level coordination - District hospital reporting - Community health worker network
Data Utilization: - Epidemic response - Policy formulation - Resource allocation - International aid coordination - Evidence-based planning

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Summary: Surveillance & Monitoring
Key Takeaways


11 Surveillance Activities: - Source approval - Watershed protection - Procedures compliance - Sanitary surveys - Monitoring programs

Surveillance Methods: - Sampling protocols - Bacteriological testing - Chemical monitoring - Quality assurance - Rapid testing


End Goal: Safe drinking water through continuous oversight

Purpose of Water Treatment

Primary Goal: Convert raw water into safe, wholesome water suitable for drinking


Three Main Objectives: 1. Remove Physical Impurities (sediment, turbidity) 2. Eliminate Biological Threats (bacteria, viruses, protozoa) 3. Reduce Chemical Contaminants (heavy metals, salts)

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
Stage 1: Storage & Sedimentation
Purpose & Process
Primary Benefits: - Removes ~90% suspended impurities in 24 hours - Allows time for settling under gravity - Reduces load on downstream filters - Cost-effective natural purification
Physical Changes: - Clear water formation (better light penetration) - Turbidity reduction - Improved conditions for UV disinfection

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
Storage: Chemical Changes
Oxidation & Bacterial Reduction
Chemical Processes: - Aerobic bacteria oxidize organic matter - Free ammonia converts to nitrates - Dissolved oxygen is consumed - pH stabilizes
Microbiological Purification: - Total bacterial count drops by 90% in 5-7 days - Pathogenic organisms gradually die out - Viruses show significant reduction - Optimal storage period: 10-14 days (river water)
⚠️ Caution: - Prolonged storage (>14 days) allows algae growth - Bad odors and color develop - Balance needed between purification and degradation

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
Storage Infrastructure
Impounding Reservoirs & Tanks
Impounding Reservoirs: - Large earthwork or masonry structures - Store significant water volumes - Suitable for urban systems - Cities: Mumbai, Chennai, Nagpur
Household/Community Tanks: - Overhead ground-level storage - Rooftop collection systems - Simple gravity-fed distribution - Requires protection from contamination
Key Requirement: Covered storage to prevent re-contamination

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
Stage 2: Filtration - Overview
Two Main Filtration Types


Slow Sand Filter (SSF)

Biological process
Gravity-driven
No chemicals needed
Low maintenance
Ideal for rural areas


Rapid Sand Filter (RSF)

Mechanical process
Chemical pre-treatment required
Regular backwashing needed
Higher operational cost
Best for urban systems


Key Principle: Filtration removes 98-99% of bacteria

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
SSF: Slow Sand Filtration
Operating Characteristics
Flow Rate: 0.1-0.4 mm/hour (very slow)
Sand Specifications: - Grain size: 0.2-0.4 mm (fine sand) - Depth: 0.5-1.5 meters - Supported by gravel layer (30-40 cm) - Total surface area: ~15,000 m² per m³
Filtration Duration: 24-72 hours for water to pass through
Pathogen Removal: 90-99% bacterial reduction

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
SSF: The Schmutzdecke Layer
Biological Magic
What is Schmutzdecke? - Biologically active layer at sand surface - Forms naturally within 2-3 weeks - Contains: - Algae (photosynthetic) - Protozoa (predatory) - Bacteria (beneficial)
How it Works: 1. Mechanical straining - Removes large particles 2. Adsorption - Traps fine particles & some chemicals 3. Biochemical degradation - Microbes break down organics 4. Predation - Protozoa consume bacteria & viruses
Result: Enhanced pathogen removal compared to sand alone

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
SSF: Process Flow
Water Journey Through SSF
Raw Water (from source)
        ↓
[Supernatant Layer - 1-1.5m]
(waiting period: 3-12 hours)
        ↓
[Schmutzdecke - biologically active layer]
        ↓
[Sand Bed - 1 meter of fine sand]
(mechanical, adsorption, oxidation)
        ↓
[Gravel Support Layer - 30-40cm]
        ↓
[Under-Drainage System]
        ↓
Purified Water

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
SSF: Advantages & Disadvantages
Comparative Analysis
Advantages: - ✓ Simple, low-cost technology - ✓ Minimal energy required (gravity-fed) - ✓ No chemicals needed - ✓ Sustainable for small communities - ✓ Highly effective (90-99% removal) - ✓ Low operational expertise required
Disadvantages: - ✗ Requires significant land area - ✗ Slow process (24-72 hours) - ✗ Maintenance needed (schmutzdecke scraping) - ✗ Ineffective for high-turbidity water - ✗ Long startup period (2-3 weeks for biofilm)

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
SSF: Maintenance & Operation
Regular Care Requirements
Schmutzdecke Maintenance: - Scrape top 5-10cm every 2-3 months - Remove accumulated debris - Biological layer regenerates within days
Sand Replacement: - Top sand layer removed during scraping - Replace periodically (every few years) - Bottom sand layers remain intact
Health Benefits Achieved: - Removes bacteria, protozoa, some viruses - Reduces turbidity significantly - Improves taste & odor - Simple monitoring for effectiveness

text:
RSF: Rapid Sand Filtration
Operating Characteristics
Flow Rate: 5-15 mm/hour (much faster than SSF)
Sand Specifications: - Grain size: 0.4-0.7 mm (coarser than SSF) - Depth: 0.5-1.5 meters - Supported by gravel layer - Allows faster water passage
Filtration Duration: 2-8 hours (major advantage)
Pathogen Removal: 95-98% with pre-treatment

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
RSF: Multi-Stage Process
Pre-Treatment is Essential
Stage 1: Coagulation-Flocculation - Chemical coagulants added (alum, ferric sulfate) - Small particles aggregate into larger flocs - Duration: 15-30 minutes - Essential for water clarity
Stage 2: Sedimentation - Flocs settle under gravity - Large particles removed - Duration: 2-4 hours - Reduces filter loading
Stage 3: Rapid Filtration - Water passes through sand - Mechanical straining - Duration: 2-8 hours - High throughput achieved

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
RSF: Maintenance Demands
Operational Complexity
Regular Backwashing: - Required every 5-15 days - Reverses water flow through sand - Removes trapped particles - Duration: 10-20 minutes - Energy intensive (requires pumps)
Chemical Management: - Coagulants must be monitored - Dosage adjusted based on water quality - Additional cost for chemicals - Trained operators needed
Troubleshooting: - Filter runs clogged → backwash - Poor water quality → adjust coagulant - Increased turbidity → check pre-treatment

Urban Household Storage: - Overhead water tanks (RCC, plastic) - Covered ground-level tanks - Individual water purifiers with storage - Building-level sump & overhead systems

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
Reverse Osmosis (RO) Systems
Advanced Household Technology
Mechanism: - Semipermeable membrane with pore size: 0.001 micrometers (1 nanometer) - Water forced through under pressure - Removes dissolved salts, heavy metals - Contaminant removal capability: >99%
Effectiveness: - ✓ Removes fluoride, arsenic, lead, nitrates - ✓ Desalination capable - ✓ Improves taste significantly
Limitations: - ✗ Wastewater generation (3:1 ratio - 3L rejected per 1L purified) - ✗ Removes beneficial minerals - ✗ Higher cost - ✗ Requires maintenance & filter replacement

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
Solar-Powered Water Systems
Renewable Energy Integration
Solar Disinfection (SODIS): - UV-A radiation + heat - Clear PET bottle in sunlight - Minimum exposure: 30 minutes optimal - Effective against bacteria, some viruses - NOT effective against: Cryptosporidium, Ascaris
Solar Pumping: - Photovoltaic panels power pumps - Drives water through RO/UV systems - Sustainable for off-grid areas
Advantages: - ✓ No electricity costs - ✓ Scalable from household to community - ✓ Sustainable technology - ✓ Ideal for rural/remote areas
Limitations: - ✗ Weather dependent - ✗ Lower effectiveness on cloudy days - ✗ May require backup system

Stage 3: Disinfection Methods
Purpose & Types
Primary Goal: Eliminate remaining pathogenic microorganisms
Five Main Methods:

Boiling
Chlorination
UV Radiation
Ozonation
Solar Disinfection (SODIS)

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
Disinfection Method 1: Boiling
Heat-Based Inactivation
Process: - Rolling boil for 10-20 minutes - All pathogens killed at 100°C - Exception: Clostridium (sporulating organisms) may survive
Advantages: - ✓ Simple, no equipment needed - ✓ Effective against all microorganisms - ✓ No residual chemicals - ✓ Affordable (fuel-dependent) - ✓ Universal acceptance
Disadvantages: - ✗ Energy intensive - ✗ No residual protection (water recontaminates) - ✗ Taste becomes bland - ✗ Not practical for large volumes
Best Use: Individual household, emergencies, bottled water

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
Disinfection Method 2: Chlorination
Chemical Disinfection - Most Widely Used
Forms of Chlorine: - Bleaching powder - Chlorine tablets/solution - Sodium hypochlorite - High test hypochlorite (HTH)
Typical Dosage: - Residual chlorine: 0.3-0.5 mg/L - Contact time: 30 minutes minimum - Adjusted based on water quality
Advantages: - ✓ Most widely used globally - ✓ Cost-effective - ✓ Provides residual protection - ✓ Effective against bacteria & viruses - ✓ Scalable (household to municipality)
Limitations: - ✗ Does NOT affect: HIV, Polio, Shigella, Salmonella, Cryptosporidium at normal doses - ✗ Forms disinfection by-products (DBPs) - ✗ Taste & odor (chlorine smell) - ✗ Requires careful dosing

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
Disinfection Method 3: UV Radiation
Light-Based Inactivation
Mechanism: - UV-A/UV-C radiation damages DNA/RNA - Microorganisms cannot reproduce - Kills bacteria & viruses effectively
Advantages: - ✓ No chemicals used - ✓ No harmful by-products - ✓ Effective against most pathogens - ✓ No taste/odor changes - ✓ Rapid disinfection
Disadvantages: - ✗ No residual protection (water recontaminates during distribution) - ✗ Requires electricity - ✗ Ineffective if water turbid (particles block UV) - ✗ Higher initial cost - ✗ Lamp maintenance needed
Best Use: Small communities, household systems with post-treatment storage protection

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
Disinfection Method 4: Ozonation
Advanced Oxidation
Mechanism: - Ozone (O₃) oxidizes organic & microbial cell membranes - Very powerful disinfectant - Converts back to O₂ (no residue)
Effectiveness: - More effective than chlorination - Works against resistant pathogens - Removes some chemicals/odors
Advantages: - ✓ Powerful disinfection - ✓ No residual toxic by-products - ✓ Improves taste & odor
Disadvantages: - ✗ Expensive technology - ✗ No residual protection - ✗ Ozone is toxic (requires containment) - ✗ Requires skilled operators - ✗ Not suitable for small communities
Best Use: Large urban systems with other technologies

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
Disinfection Method 5: Solar Disinfection (SODIS)
Household-Level Solar Method
Requirements: - Clear PET plastic bottles - Sunlight exposure - Minimum 30 minutes (longer on cloudy days)
Process: - UV-A radiation + heat (60-65°C) - Kills bacteria & viruses - Some viral inactivation
Effectiveness: - ✓ Bacteria: highly effective - ✓ Viruses: effective - ✗ Protozoa: NOT effective (Cryptosporidium, Ascaris resistant)
Advantages: - ✓ Zero cost - ✓ No chemicals - ✓ Accessible to poorest communities - ✓ Simple to implement
Limitations: - ✗ Weather dependent - ✗ Not effective against all pathogens - ✗ Time-consuming - ✗ Limited to small quantities

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
section: WHO Guidelines for Drinking Water Quality
text:
WHO Guidelines for Drinking Water Quality
Overview and Evolution
Purpose:
Define standards for countries to develop national regulations ensuring safe drinking water supplies.
Publication History:

1984: First edition published
1993: Vol. 1 of 2nd edition
1996: Vol. 2 of 2nd edition
2011: Vol. 1 & II of 3rd edition ⭐ (current standard)
2017: Updated addendum

Key Principle:
Standards must consider local environmental, social, economic, and cultural contexts—not one-size-fits-all.
Four Aspects of Water Quality:

Acceptability aspects (Physical + Inorganic)
Microbiological aspects
Chemical aspects (Inorganic + Organic + Pesticides)
Radiological aspects


The WHO guidelines are recommendations, not mandatory regulations. Each country adapts them based on local conditions, resources, and priorities. India’s standards (IS 10500) largely align with WHO but have some variations based on endemic conditions (e.g., fluoride).

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
I. Acceptability Aspects
A. Physical Parameters
Definition: Characteristics affecting water’s aesthetic quality and acceptability to consumers.
Key Parameters:








Parameter
Acceptable Limit
Health/Aesthetic Impact




Turbidity
<5 NTU (Nephelometric Turbidity Units)
>5 NTU visible cloudiness, shields pathogens from disinfection


Colour
<15 TCU (True Colour Units)
Indicates organic matter, iron, or manganese contamination


Taste and Odour
No objectionable taste/odour
May indicate organic decay, hydrogen sulfide, or chlorination by-products


Temperature
<25°C
High temp reduces dissolved oxygen, increases microbial growth



Significance:
Even if microbiologically safe, water with poor acceptability aspects may cause consumers to seek unsafe alternative sources.

Turbidity is critical—particles shield bacteria from chlorine disinfection. Studies show that reducing turbidity from 5 NTU to 1 NTU can increase disinfection efficacy by 90%. Consumers often prefer clear water even if unsafe, rejecting turbid water even if treated.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
II. Microbiological Aspects
Bacteriological Indicators
Why Indicators?
Testing for all pathogens is impractical. Indicators signal fecal contamination and potential presence of pathogens.
Primary Indicator: Coliform Organisms

Total Coliforms: Gram-negative, lactose-fermenting bacteria (includes E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter)
Fecal Coliforms (Thermotolerant): Ferment lactose at 44°C; E. coli is the primary member
Escherichia coli: Definitive indicator of recent fecal contamination

Guideline: - Drinking water: 0 E. coli or fecal coliforms per 100 mL - Treated water entering distribution: 0 coliforms per 100 mL - Treated water in distribution: <3 coliforms per 100 mL (if chlorine residual present)
Other Indicators:

Faecal Streptococci (Enterococcus): More persistent than coliforms, indicates older contamination
Clostridium perfringens: Spore-forming; indicates remote or intermittent contamination


E. coli is the gold standard fecal indicator because: (1) exclusively of fecal origin, (2) doesn’t multiply in water, (3) easy to detect, (4) outnumbers pathogens 1000:1. However, it doesn’t indicate protozoa or viruses, which are more chlorine-resistant.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
Polynuclear Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs)
Coal-Tar Contamination and Cancer Risk
What are PAHs?
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons formed during incomplete combustion of organic materials: - Coal, oil, wood, garbage burning - Vehicle exhaust - Industrial processes - Cigarette smoke
Major PAHs in Water:

Benzo[a]pyrene (BaP): Most potent carcinogen, guideline = 0.7 µg/L
Benzo[b]fluoranthene, Benzo[k]fluoranthene
Indeno[1,2,3-cd]pyrene
Dibenz[a,h]anthracene

WHO Recommendations for PAH Control:

Turbidity Reduction: PAHs adsorb to suspended particles. Reducing turbidity removes PAHs.
Ban Coal-Tar Materials: Discontinue use of coal-tar-based materials for pipe lining and storage tank coatings—major contamination source.
Source Identification: When PAH contamination detected, identify specific compounds and sources, as carcinogenic potential varies.


The 1970s-80s saw widespread PAH contamination from coal-tar pipe linings in U.S. and Europe. Decades later, elevated cancer rates appeared. WHO recommends removing old coal-tar pipes. In India, some old municipal systems still have coal-tar linings, requiring monitoring.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
Health-Risk Assessment Framework
Understanding TDI, ADI, NOAEL, LOAEL
Why Risk Assessment?
Cannot test every chemical on humans ethically. Must extrapolate from animal studies to establish safe limits.
Key Concepts:
1. Tolerable Daily Intake (TDI)

Maximum amount of a substance a person can consume daily over a lifetime without appreciable health risk
Expressed as mg/kg body weight/day

2. Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI)

Similar to TDI but used for food additives and pesticides (intentional additions)
TDI used for contaminants (unintentional)

3. No-Observed-Adverse-Effect Level (NOAEL)

Highest dose in animal studies where NO adverse effects detected
Basis for deriving TDI

4. Lowest-Observed-Adverse-Effect Level (LOAEL)

Lowest dose in animal studies where adverse effects ARE detected
Used when NOAEL data unavailable (with additional uncertainty factor)


Example: Arsenic NOAEL study on rats might find 0.3 mg/kg bw/day causes no tumors. But humans may be more sensitive, so we apply uncertainty factors (typically 100-1000) to derive a safe TDI. This conservative approach protects public health given scientific uncertainties.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
Uncertainty Factors (UF)
Accounting for Variability and Unknowns
Purpose:
Account for uncertainties when extrapolating from animal studies to human populations.
Four Sources of Uncertainty:








Source
Uncertainty Factor Range
Rationale




Interspecies variation
1 - 10
Animals may respond differently than humans


Intraspecies variation
1 - 10
Humans vary (children, elderly, sick more sensitive)


Adequacy of studies
1 - 10
Short-term study → lifetime exposure extrapolation


Nature/severity of effect
1 - 10
Severe effects (cancer) require more caution



Total UF Calculation:
UF (total) = UF₁ × UF₂ × UF₃ × UF₄
Typical Values:

100: Standard for well-studied chemicals (10 × 10: interspecies × intraspecies)
1000: Additional factor when using LOAEL instead of NOAEL
10,000: Maximum; higher values make TDI too imprecise (guideline becomes “provisional”)


Example: Arsenic uses UF=100 (10 interspecies × 10 intraspecies) because we have good human epidemiological data. Lead uses higher UF because children are especially vulnerable (neurodevelopment). The WHO expert panel determines UF by consensus, reviewing all available evidence.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
Deriving Guideline Values Using TDI
Step-by-Step Calculation
Formula 1: Calculate TDI
TDI (mg/kg bw/day) = NOAEL (or LOAEL) / UF
Formula 2: Calculate Guideline Value (GV)
GV (mg/L) = (TDI × bw × P) / C
Where:

bw = Body weight (60 kg adult, 10 kg child, 5 kg infant)
P = Fraction of TDI allocated to drinking water (typically 0.1 or 10%)
C = Daily drinking water consumption (2 L adult, 1 L child, 0.75 L infant)

Why P = 0.1?
Most chemicals come from multiple sources (food, air, soil). Water typically contributes 10-20% of total exposure. For chemicals exclusively in water (e.g., disinfection by-products), P may be higher (0.8).

The allocation factor P is critical. For lead, P=0.5 (50%) because drinking water is a major source for infants. For pesticides, P=0.1 (10%) because food is the primary source. When deriving guideline values, we must consider all exposure routes, not just water.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
Worked Example: Arsenic Guideline Value
Applying the TDI Approach
Given Data:

NOAEL (from animal studies) = 0.3 mg/kg bw/day
Uncertainty Factor (UF) = 100 (10 interspecies × 10 intraspecies)
Allocation to water (P) = 0.1 (10%)
Body weight (bw) = 60 kg (adult)
Water consumption (C) = 2 L/day

Step 1: Calculate TDI
TDI <- NOAEL / UF
TDI <- 0.3 / 100
TDI <- 0.003 mg/kg bw/day
Step 2: Calculate Guideline Value
GV <- (TDI * bw * P) / C
GV <- (0.003 * 60 * 0.1) / 2
GV <- 0.018 / 2
GV <- 0.009 mg/L = 9 µg/L
WHO Guideline: 0.01 mg/L (10 µg/L) — rounded for practical monitoring

WHO’s arsenic guideline (10 µg/L) is based on epidemiological studies in Bangladesh, Taiwan, and Chile showing skin lesions and cancers. The calculation here is simplified; actual derivation considered multiple studies, exposure routes, and cancer risk models. Some countries (Bangladesh) use 50 µg/L as an interim target due to widespread natural contamination.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
IV. Radiological Aspects
Radioactivity in Drinking Water
What is Radioactivity?
Nuclear disintegration of unstable isotopes, releasing ionizing radiation (alpha, beta, gamma particles).
Unit of Activity:

Becquerel (Bq): 1 disintegration per second (modern unit)
Curie (Ci): 3.7 × 10¹⁰ disintegrations per second (old unit)
1 Ci = 37 GBq

WHO Guideline Values:








Indicator
Guideline Value
Rationale




Gross Alpha Activity
0.5 Bq/L
Screening for α-emitters (radon, radium, uranium)


Gross Beta Activity
1.0 Bq/L
Screening for β-emitters (cesium-137, strontium-90, tritium)



If screening levels exceeded: Identify specific radionuclides and assess individual dose contribution.

Radiological contamination comes from natural (uranium, radium in rocks) or anthropogenic (nuclear facilities, medical waste) sources. Alpha emitters are more biologically damaging than beta/gamma due to high energy in short range. Radon (gas) from uranium decay in groundwater is a common concern in granite regions.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
Radiological Health Effects
Somatic vs. Hereditary, Stochastic vs. Non-Stochastic
Types of Effects:
1. Somatic Effects (manifest in exposed individual) - Acute: Radiation sickness, burns (high dose, short time) - Delayed: Cancer, cataracts, cardiovascular disease
2. Hereditary Effects (affect descendants) - Genetic mutations passed to offspring - Risk increases with gonadal dose
Dose-Response Relationships:
Stochastic Effects: - Probability increases with dose (no threshold) - Severity constant - Example: Cancer risk (0.05% per mSv for solid cancers)
Non-Stochastic (Deterministic) Effects: - Severity increases with dose (threshold exists) - Example: Cataracts (threshold ~2 Gy), skin burns
Radiation Protection Principle:
Keep exposures As Low As Reasonably Achievable (ALARA), even below guideline limits.

There’s no “safe” dose for stochastic effects (cancer)—risk exists at any exposure. Guideline values represent acceptable risk (typically <10⁻⁴ additional lifetime cancer risk). Non-stochastic effects have thresholds; below threshold, no effect occurs. Water guidelines aim to prevent deterministic effects and minimize stochastic risk.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
Long Answer Questions (10 marks each)

Describe the WHO Guidelines for Drinking Water Quality (2011), including the four aspects of water quality. For each aspect, list key parameters and their health significance. Explain why context-specific adaptation is necessary.
Explain the health-risk assessment framework used to derive drinking water guideline values. Define TDI, NOAEL, LOAEL, and Uncertainty Factors. Illustrate with a worked example calculating a guideline value from NOAEL.
Discuss organic constituents of health concern in drinking water, including chlorinated alkanes, aromatic hydrocarbons, and polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). Explain sources, health effects, and WHO recommendations for PAH control.

Explain radiological aspects of drinking water quality. Define gross alpha and beta activity, discuss sources of radioactive contamination, differentiate between somatic and hereditary effects, and explain stochastic vs. non-stochastic effects.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
text:
Welcome to Module 2
Environment & Health Fundamentals
Learning Objectives:

Define environment and its three components (physical, biologic, social)
Understand the relationship between environmental factors and human health
Explain the concept of sanitation and environmental health
Identify major environmental hazards threatening human health
Describe the evolution from environmental sanitation to environmental health
Recognize the role of multi-disciplinary approaches in environmental health


This module establishes the foundational concepts of environmental health that underpin all subsequent discussions on water, sanitation, and public health interventions.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
text:
Review: One Health MCQs
Question 1
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) spreads through water systems primarily due to:

Inadequate chlorination of drinking water
Excretion of antibiotics from livestock entering agricultural runoff
Natural bacterial mutations in water bodies
Industrial chemical contamination


Explanation: 75-90% of antibiotics given to livestock are excreted unchanged and enter water systems through manure and agricultural runoff, spreading resistant bacteria and resistance genes (Module 1 content).

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
text:
What is Environment?
Modern Concept of Environment

“The study of disease is really the study of man and his environment”

Definition:
Environment comprises all external factors—living and non-living, material and non-material—that surround humans and influence health outcomes.
Traditional View: - Water, air, soil
Modern View: - Physical environment (water, air, soil, housing, radiation) - Biological environment (plants, animals, microorganisms) - Social environment (customs, culture, income, occupation, religion)
Key Recognition: Health is determined not just by biological factors but by the total environment in which humans live.

The modern concept of environment expands beyond natural elements to include socioeconomic determinants. For example, poor housing (physical) combined with low income (social) and rat infestation (biological) interact to cause leptospirosis outbreaks.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
text:
Three Components of Environment
1. Physical Environment
Elements: - Water: Quality, quantity, accessibility - Air: Pollution, composition, ventilation - Soil: Contamination, fertility - Housing: Overcrowding, ventilation, construction materials - Wastes: Solid, liquid, hazardous waste disposal - Radiation: Ionizing, non-ionizing sources
Health Impact: Water contamination (diarrheal diseases), air pollution (respiratory diseases), poor housing (communicable diseases)
Control Measures: Engineering solutions, regulations, monitoring systems

Physical environment factors are often most amenable to control through engineering interventions (water treatment plants, sewage systems, air quality monitoring). However, effectiveness depends on maintenance and community participation.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
text:
Ill-Health and Environmental Factors
Environmental Hazards to Human Health
Major Adverse Factors:

Water Pollution

Biological (pathogens)
Chemical (heavy metals, nitrates, fluorides)
Physical (turbidity, temperature)

Soil Pollution

Pesticides, fertilizers
Industrial effluents
Solid waste contamination

Air Pollution

Indoor (cooking smoke, poor ventilation)
Outdoor (vehicular emissions, industrial fumes)

Poor Housing

Overcrowding (tuberculosis, skin diseases)
Inadequate ventilation (respiratory infections)
Lack of sanitation facilities

Disease Vectors & Reservoirs

Mosquitoes, flies, rodents
Animal reservoirs (livestock, wildlife)



Much of human ill-health can be traced to adverse environmental factors. The 1972 UN Conference on Human Environment brought global attention to these hazards. WHO’s survey identified hundreds of environmental risks, with water and sanitation being among the most critical.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
text:
Human-Induced Environmental Pollution
The Role of Urbanization & Industrialization
Human Activities Polluting Environment:

Urbanization: Overcrowding, inadequate infrastructure, slums
Industrialization: Chemical effluents, air emissions, hazardous waste
Agricultural Intensification: Pesticides, fertilizers, animal waste
Deforestation: Loss of natural purification systems
Waste Generation: Plastics, e-waste, medical waste

Consequences:








Activity
Environmental Impact
Health Impact




Industrial waste discharge
River pollution
Waterborne diseases, heavy metal toxicity


Vehicle emissions
Air pollution
Respiratory diseases, cardiovascular diseases


Excessive fertilizer use
Groundwater nitrate contamination
Methemoglobinemia in infants


Urban sprawl
Habitat disruption
Emergence of zoonotic diseases



1972 UN Conference: Focused worldwide attention on environmental hazards threatening human beings.

Man is often responsible for his own environmental problems. Rapid industrialization without adequate pollution control has led to severe environmental degradation in India. Rivers like Yamuna and Ganga are heavily polluted despite their cultural significance. Addressing pollution requires balancing economic development with environmental protection.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
text:
What is Sanitation?
Evolution of the Concept
Dictionary Definition: “The science of safeguarding health”
National Sanitation Foundation (USA) Definition:

“Sanitation is a way of life. It is the quality of living that is expressed in the clean home, the clean farm, the clean business, the clean neighbourhood and the clean community. Being a way of life, it must come from within the people; it is nourished by knowledge and grows as an obligation and an ideal in human relations.”

Historical Perspective: - Past: Centered on sanitary disposal of human excreta (latrines) - Present: Comprehensive control of all environmental factors affecting health
Key Point: Sanitation is not just infrastructure—it’s a behavior, a culture, a way of life.

Many people still equate sanitation with toilet construction. However, modern sanitation encompasses food safety, water quality, waste management, vector control, housing, and personal hygiene. Sustainable sanitation requires community ownership and behavior change, not just infrastructure.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
text:
Environmental Sanitation (WHO Definition)
Scope of Control
WHO Definition:

“Environmental sanitation is the control of all those factors in man’s physical environment which exercise or may exercise a deleterious effect on his physical development, health and survival.”

Controllable Environmental Factors (Standard of Living):

Food: Safety, nutritional quality, availability
Water: Quality, quantity, accessibility
Housing: Adequate, ventilated, uncrowded
Clothing: Protection from climate, hygiene
Sanitation: Excreta disposal, solid waste management

Historical Impact:
Control of these factors in developed countries during the 19th-20th centuries led to dramatic health improvements—even before antibiotics and vaccines.

The sanitary revolution (clean water, sewage systems) in Europe and North America reduced mortality more than medical interventions. For example, London’s 1854 cholera outbreak (John Snow) was controlled by removing a contaminated water pump handle—demonstrating the power of environmental control.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
section: From Environmental Sanitation to Environmental Health
text:
From Environmental Sanitation to Environmental Health
The Evolution
Old Problems Being Solved: - Excreta disposal (latrines, sewage treatment) - Safe water supply (treatment plants, distribution) - Vector control (DDT, insecticides—though with new challenges)
New Problems Arising:

Air Pollution: Rapid urbanization, vehicular growth
Industrial Pollution: Chemical effluents, hazardous waste
Radioactive Pollution: Nuclear technology advances
Demographic Growth: Population pressure on resources
Rapid Urbanization: Slums, inadequate infrastructure
E-waste: Electronic waste management challenges

Consequence: Environmental sanitation → Environmental Health (broader, complex)

As societies solve old problems, new challenges emerge. For example, India has increased latrine coverage through Swachh Bharat Mission, but now faces challenges with sewage treatment and fecal sludge management. Air pollution in Delhi rivals Beijing. The term “environmental health” reflects the growing complexity and need for integrated solutions.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
text:
Multi-Disciplinary Approach to Environmental Health
Who is Involved?
Traditional Approach: - Medical professionals (diagnosis, treatment) - Engineers (infrastructure design)
Modern Environmental Health Requires:

Public Health Physicians: Disease surveillance, policy
Epidemiologists: Disease patterns, outbreak investigation
Public Health Engineers: Water treatment, sanitation systems
Town Planners: Urban design, zoning
Sociologists: Community behavior, cultural practices
Economists: Cost-benefit analysis, financing
Health Inspectors: Monitoring, enforcement
Environmental Scientists: Pollution assessment, ecology

Key Message: Neither purely medical nor purely engineering—requires combined, multi-disciplinary action.

The COVID-19 pandemic exemplified the need for multi-disciplinary response: epidemiologists tracked spread, clinicians treated patients, engineers designed ventilation in hospitals, sociologists addressed vaccine hesitancy, economists managed financial impacts, and public health officials coordinated policy. No single discipline can address complex environmental health challenges.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
text:
Purpose of Environmental Health
Creating Healthy Ecological Conditions
Primary Goal:
Create and maintain ecological conditions that will promote health and prevent disease.
Essential Elements:

Safe Drinking Water: Free from biological and chemical contaminants
Adequate Sanitation: Excreta disposal systems preventing disease transmission
Solid Waste Management: Collection, treatment, disposal
Vector Control: Reducing disease-carrying organisms
Food Safety: Prevention of food-borne illnesses
Air Quality: Reducing indoor and outdoor pollution
Occupational Health: Safe working environments

Global Challenge (1990s): - >1 billion people lacked safe drinking water - ~2 billion lacked adequate sanitation - Faeces near homes, contaminated water, polluted fish/produce = health hazards

Safe water and sanitation are fundamental human rights (UN General Assembly, 2010). Yet billions still lack access. Water quantity is as important as quality—without abundant water near the home, hygiene becomes impossible. Washing hands after defecation requires adequate water supply.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
text:
Water Quantity and Quality
Both are Essential
Water Quantity:

Minimum survival: ~3-5 liters/person/day
Basic needs: 20-50 liters/person/day
Adequate supply (urban India): 150-200 liters/person/day
Rural India target: 40 liters/person/day

Importance of Quantity:

Washing hands after defecation
Bathing and personal hygiene
Cooking and food preparation
Cleaning utensils and surfaces
Laundry

Water Quality:
Must be free from: - Pathogenic microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, protozoa, helminths) - Toxic chemicals (arsenic, fluoride, nitrates, heavy metals) - Excessive turbidity, color, odor
Key Insight: Without abundant water in or near the home, hygiene becomes difficult or impossible—even if the water is microbiologically safe.

Studies show that proximity to water source matters more than water quality for health outcomes. Families with water far from home reduce consumption to conserve energy, compromising hygiene. A safe water source 1 km away is less effective than a moderately safe source 50 meters away, because quantity enables hygiene practices.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
text:
Environmental Diseases in Developing Countries
The Burden of Poor Sanitation
Major Disease Categories:

Diarrheal Diseases (10% of total disease burden)

Cholera, typhoid, dysentery
Rotavirus, E. coli infections
Giardiasis, amebiasis

Intestinal Worm Infestations

Ascariasis (roundworm)
Hookworm
Tapeworm infections

Water-Washed Diseases (inadequate water for hygiene)

Trachoma (leading cause of preventable blindness)
Scabies, skin infections
Conjunctivitis

Water-Based Diseases

Schistosomiasis (bilharzia)
Guinea worm disease (dracunculiasis)

Water-Related Vector Diseases

Malaria, dengue, filariasis (mosquitoes)
Japanese encephalitis



The lack of water supply and sanitation is the primary reason why faecal-oral diseases are so common in developing countries. Even diseases not classified as “waterborne” (like trachoma) are heavily influenced by water availability for hygiene. Eliminating these diseases requires both safe water AND adequate quantity.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
section: Access to Safe Water and Sanitation in South-East Asia

India’s 94% rural access to safe water (Census 2011) is misleading—it includes unprotected sources and doesn’t account for seasonal availability or water quality. Similarly, having a toilet (Swachh Bharat achievement) doesn’t mean it’s used or that waste is safely managed. Behavior change and maintenance are as critical as infrastructure.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
text:
Achieving “Health for All”
Two Critical Changes Needed
From WHO’s “Health for All” Strategy:
1. Healthy Environment - Safe water and sanitation - Clean air quality - Safe food supply - Vector control - Solid waste management - Requires: Government policy, infrastructure investment, regulation enforcement
2. Healthy Lifestyle - Personal hygiene practices - Proper food handling - Hand washing at critical times - Safe drinking water storage - Sanitary behaviors - Requires: Individual initiative, family participation, community action, health education
Key Insight: Both changes are essential and interdependent. Infrastructure without behavior change = wasted investment. Education without infrastructure = frustration.

The failure of many WASH programs stems from focusing on only one aspect. Building toilets without addressing open defecation norms fails (India’s experience). Conversely, teaching hand washing without providing nearby water sources is ineffective. Successful programs integrate infrastructure, education, and community mobilization.

title: Module 2: Environment & Health Fundamentals
text:
Module 2 Summary
Key Takeaways
Core Concepts:
✓ Environment includes physical, biological, and social components—all affecting health
✓ Much of human ill-health traces to adverse environmental factors (water, air, soil, housing, vectors)
✓ Humans are responsible for environmental pollution through urbanization and industrialization
✓ Sanitation is a way of life, not just infrastructure—requires knowledge and community ownership
✓ Environmental health requires multi-disciplinary approaches (medical, engineering, social)
✓ Safe water and adequate sanitation are fundamental to public health
✓ Both water quantity and quality are essential for hygiene and disease prevention
Next Steps:
Module 3 will dive deep into water quality standards and criteria, covering WHO guidelines, chemical parameters, and health-risk assessment methods.

text:

Question 1
Which component of environment is the MOST difficult to change but often most critical for health outcomes?

Physical environment
Biological environment
Social environment
None of the above


Explanation: Social environment (customs, culture, income, education) is hardest to change because it involves deep-rooted behaviors and beliefs. However, it’s often most critical—for example, even with toilet infrastructure, open defecation continues if social norms don’t change. Physical and biological factors are more amenable to engineering solutions.

title: Disaster Management
text:
Welcome
Disaster Management
Learning Objectives:

Classify disasters as natural vs. man-made, and internal vs. external
Describe the four phases of the disaster management cycle
Outline India’s Disaster Management Act, 2005 and its authority structure
Apply the levels-of-prevention framework to disaster mitigation

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter reuses the levels-of-prevention framework (Chapter 2) in a new context: mitigation and preparedness act before a disaster’s “pathogenesis,” while response and recovery act after.

title: Disaster Management
text:
Classifying Disasters
🟢 MUST KNOW

Natural disasters — arising from forces of nature: weather events (cyclones, floods, droughts), geological events (earthquakes, landslides), and epidemiological events (epidemics)
Man-made disasters — directly attributable to human action: armed conflict, industrial/technological accidents (e.g. chemical or nuclear incidents), severe pollution, and bioterrorism

A second, independent classification by location:

Internal disasters — occur within a health facility itself (power outage, fire, cyberattack on hospital records)
External disasters — occur outside, but generate casualties the health system must absorb (transportation accidents, industrial incidents, natural disasters)

title: Disaster Management
text:
The Disaster Management Cycle
🟢 MUST KNOW
A continuous, four-phase cycle — each phase informs the next:

Mitigation — reducing vulnerability before any disaster occurs (building codes, zoning, strengthening infrastructure)
Preparedness — building capacity to respond and recover (training, planning, stockpiling, early warning systems)
Response — actions taken during/immediately after a disaster to save lives, reduce losses, and relieve suffering
Recovery — restoring the community to pre-disaster (or better) functioning

Direct parallel to Chapter 2’s levels of prevention: mitigation and preparedness are essentially primary prevention applied to disasters; response is analogous to acute case management; recovery parallels tertiary prevention (limiting long-term disability/impact).

title: Disaster Management
text:
India’s Disaster Management Act, 2005
🟢 MUST KNOW
Enacted 23 December 2005, providing India’s legal and institutional framework for disaster management, with 11 chapters and 79 sections, establishing a multi-tiered authority structure:

National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) — the apex body, headed by the Prime Minister, laying down policies, plans, and guidelines
State Disaster Management Authorities (SDMAs) — state-level equivalent
District Disaster Management Authorities (DDMAs) — district-level implementation

National Executive Committee (NEC) — coordinates the national response and prepares the National Plan, working alongside NDMA.

title: Disaster Management
section: Health System’s Role Across the Cycle
text:
Health System’s Role Across the Cycle
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
The health sector has specific responsibilities at every phase:

Mitigation — ensuring hospitals themselves are structurally resilient (a hospital that collapses in an earthquake can’t treat earthquake casualties)
Preparedness — mass-casualty triage training, stockpiling emergency medicines and supplies, disaster drills
Response — triage, emergency care, epidemic surveillance for disease outbreaks that commonly follow disasters (contaminated water, crowding — recall Chapter 6’s chain of infection)
Recovery — restoring routine health services, and addressing longer-term mental health needs of affected populations (Chapter 10)

title: Disaster Management
section: Public Health Risks After a Disaster
text:
Public Health Risks After a Disaster
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Disasters — especially floods and cyclones — create conditions that directly increase communicable disease risk:

Disrupted water and sanitation infrastructure → waterborne disease outbreaks
Overcrowding in relief shelters → increased respiratory and contact-transmitted disease spread
Disrupted immunization and health services → resurgence of vaccine-preventable disease

This is why disaster response plans integrate epidemiological surveillance (Chapter 6) as a core, not optional, component.

title: Disaster Management
text:
Slow-Onset vs. Sudden-Onset Disasters
🟣 MAY KNOW
Disasters are also distinguished by speed of onset: sudden-onset events (earthquakes, industrial explosions) demand immediate emergency response, while slow-onset events (droughts, some epidemics) unfold over weeks to months, allowing more time for anticipatory action but often receiving less public attention and funding until effects become severe.

title: Disaster Management
text:
Building Back Better
🟣 MAY KNOW
Modern disaster recovery increasingly follows a “build back better” principle — using the recovery phase not merely to restore pre-disaster conditions, but to rebuild with greater resilience against future events, integrating mitigation directly into recovery rather than treating them as fully separate cycle phases.

title: Module 2: Hypertension
text:
Welcome
Hypertension
Learning Objectives:

Describe the global and Indian burden of hypertension
Define hypertension and classify it by severity
Identify risk factors for hypertension
Apply primary and secondary prevention to hypertension control

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

Hypertension is both a disease in its own right and the single largest modifiable risk factor for stroke, covered next — the two modules are best read together.

title: Module 2: Hypertension
text:
Definition and Burden
🟢 MUST KNOW
Hypertension is diagnosed when, on two separate days, systolic BP ≥140 mmHg and/or diastolic BP ≥90 mmHg.

Global: ~1.13 billion people affected, two-thirds in low- and middle-income countries; prevalence over 60% in people aged 60+
India (NFHS 2015–16): 15% of men, 11% of women hypertensive; prevalence rises consistently with BMI
Called the “silent killer” — most affected people have no symptoms and are unaware of their status, which is why regular BP measurement matters more than symptom-based detection

Global NCD target: reduce hypertension prevalence by 25% by 2025 (2010 baseline).

title: Module 2: Hypertension
text:
Classification
🟢 MUST KNOW



Category
Systolic (mmHg)
Diastolic (mmHg)




Optimal
<120
<80

<85

Grade 1 (mild)

≥160

When symptoms do occur (usually only at higher grades): early morning headache, nosebleeds, irregular heart rhythm, vision changes, tinnitus; severe hypertension can cause fatigue, nausea, confusion, and chest pain.

title: Module 2: Hypertension
text:
Risk Factors and Prevention
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Risk factors: age, sex, genetic factors, ethnicity, obesity, high salt intake, alcohol use, physical inactivity, environmental stress.

Primary prevention — reduce population-wide incidence through low salt diet, regular exercise, stress reduction, and weight/BMI control
Secondary prevention — early case detection (routine BP screening) plus antihypertensive drug therapy once diagnosed

Treatment approach: lifestyle modification and stress management as the foundation, with antihypertensive medication (e.g. amlodipine, telmisartan, chlorthalidone — representative drug classes, not a prescribing guide) added for confirmed hypertension.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Welcome
Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
Learning Objectives:

Define non-communicable disease (NCD) and name the four major NCDs
Identify the four shared modifiable behavioural risk factors
Distinguish behavioural from metabolic/intermediate risk factors
State the global NCD targets (WHO 25x25 and SDG 3.4)
Outline India’s National Programme for Prevention and Control of NCDs
Describe the WHO STEPS surveillance approach
Explain Rose’s population strategy vs. high-risk strategy

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

Chapter 6 covered communicable disease; this chapter is its structural mirror for non-communicable disease, and reuses the levels-of-prevention and causation frameworks from the Foundations section.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
What Is a Non-Communicable Disease?
🟢 MUST KNOW
An NCD is a disease that is not directly transmissible from person to person, and typically has a long duration and slow progression, resulting from a combination of genetic, physiological, environmental, and behavioural factors.
The four major NCDs (responsible for the large majority of the global NCD burden):

Cardiovascular disease (CVD)
Cancer
Chronic respiratory disease
Diabetes mellitus

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
section: The Four Shared Behavioural Risk Factors
text:
The Four Shared Behavioural Risk Factors
🟢 MUST KNOW
The same four modifiable behaviours drive all four major NCDs, which is why NCD prevention is tackled as one integrated agenda rather than disease-by-disease:

Tobacco use
Unhealthy diet
Physical inactivity
Harmful use of alcohol

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Metabolic (Intermediate) Risk Factors
🟢 MUST KNOW
Behavioural risk factors act through measurable, intermediate biological changes:

Raised blood pressure
Overweight / obesity
Hyperglycaemia (raised blood glucose)
Hyperlipidaemia (raised blood cholesterol/lipids)

These metabolic factors are themselves the direct targets of most clinical NCD screening and management.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Global NCD Targets
🟢 MUST KNOW

WHO “25×25” target — a 25% relative reduction in premature mortality (ages 30–69) from the four major NCDs by 2025, compared with 2010 levels
SDG Target 3.4 — reduce premature NCD mortality by one-third by 2030 (relative to 2015), and promote mental health and well-being

“Premature” mortality in both targets specifically means death in the 30–69 age band — deaths that public health intervention can plausibly prevent.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
India’s Response: NP-NCD
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
India’s National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD), launched in 2010 as NPCDCS in 100 districts, has evolved considerably:
NPCDCS (2010, 100 districts) → subsumed under NHM (2013–14) → Population-Based Screening under Comprehensive Primary Health Care (2016) → National Multisectoral Action Plan (2016) → renamed NP-NCD

Focus: health promotion, screening, early diagnosis, and management of individuals with NCDs, alongside risk-factor reduction
Scope expanded in phases to include COPD/asthma, chronic kidney disease, stroke, NAFLD, and STEMI alongside the original cardiovascular disease/diabetes/cancer focus
India’s NCD burden (WHO NCD Country Profile): NCDs account for 63% of all deaths — cardiovascular disease leads (27%), followed by chronic respiratory disease (11%), cancer (9%), and diabetes (3%)

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Non-Modifiable Risk Factors
🟢 MUST KNOW
Alongside the four modifiable behaviours, NCD risk is also shaped by factors that cannot be changed:

Age — NCD risk rises with age for most conditions
Sex — some NCDs show marked sex differences in incidence
Genetics / family history — inherited susceptibility

Public health strategy focuses on the modifiable factors, but non-modifiable factors still matter for risk stratification and targeted screening.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
WHO STEPS Surveillance
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
The WHO STEPwise approach to Surveillance (STEPS) is the standard method countries use to monitor NCD risk factors, in three progressively more intensive steps:

Step 1 — Questionnaire: demographic data and behavioural risk factors (tobacco, alcohol, diet, physical activity)
Step 2 — Physical measurements: height, weight, waist circumference, blood pressure
Step 3 — Biochemical measurements: blood glucose and lipid levels

Countries can implement Step 1 alone or build up to all three, depending on resources.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Population Strategy vs. High-Risk Strategy
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Geoffrey Rose (1981) distinguished two prevention strategies:

High-risk strategy — identify and intervene on individuals at highest risk (e.g. treating severe hypertension)
Population strategy — shift the risk-factor distribution of the entire population slightly downward (e.g. a national salt-reduction policy)

Rose’s Prevention Paradox: because most cases of a common disease arise from the large number of people at moderate risk (not the small number at extreme risk), a population-wide strategy usually prevents more total disease than a high-risk strategy — even though the benefit to any one individual is small.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Double Burden of Disease
🟣 MAY KNOW
Many low- and middle-income countries, including India, now face a double burden of disease: they have not fully controlled communicable, maternal, and nutritional conditions, while NCDs are simultaneously rising — meaning health systems must manage both agendas at once, with finite resources.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Measuring NCD Burden: DALYs
🟣 MAY KNOW
The overall burden of a disease — combining both fatal and non-fatal impact — is commonly measured using Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs): years of healthy life lost to premature death plus years lived with disability. NCDs, being long-duration and disabling rather than always immediately fatal, are a major driver of global DALY burden. (Health indicators, including DALYs, are covered in more depth in the Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics chapter.)

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Explore: Selected Diseases in Depth
🟣 MAY KNOW
The principles above apply across NCDs generally — three specific diseases are covered in dedicated modules, each with burden, risk factors, screening/diagnosis, and prevention in full depth:
Diabetes Mellitus · Hypertension · Stroke
Or browse the module hub for an overview of all three.
