title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
Welcome
Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
Learning Objectives:

Define essential medicines and state WHO’s selection criteria
Describe India’s National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM)
State WHO’s definition of rational use of medicines and list forms of irrational use
Distinguish substandard, falsified, and generic medicines
Explain why WHO retired the term “counterfeit medicines”

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter shifts focus from disease epidemiology to the medicines supply chain — access, rational prescribing, and quality — as a determinant of health-system performance.

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
What Are Essential Medicines?
🟢 MUST KNOW
WHO definition: essential medicines are those that satisfy the priority health care needs of a population.
Selection criteria:

Disease prevalence and public health relevance
Evidence of clinical efficacy and safety
Comparative cost and cost-effectiveness

The first WHO Model List of Essential Drugs was published in 1977, with 186 medicines, to help countries prioritize which medicines to stock, procure, and make affordable at every level of care.

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
section: India’s National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM)
text:
India’s National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM)
🟢 MUST KNOW
India adapts the WHO model into its own National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM), maintained under the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) — India’s National Regulatory Authority.

First published 2011; most recently revised as NLEM 2022 (384 medicines across 27 therapeutic categories)
Inclusion criteria: approved/licensed in India, cost-effective, and stable under Indian storage conditions
Purpose: ensure accessibility of affordable, quality medicines at every level of healthcare, and to guide public procurement and price control

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
Rational Use of Medicines
🟢 MUST KNOW
WHO definition (1985): rational use means patients receive medications appropriate to their clinical needs, in doses that meet their individual requirements, for an adequate period of time, and at the lowest cost to them and their community.
The core criteria:

Appropriate indication
Appropriate medicine choice
Appropriate dosage
Correctly dispensed
Patient appropriately informed
Patient adherence

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
Forms of Irrational Use
🟢 MUST KNOW
Common patterns of irrational medicine use:

Polypharmacy — using too many medicines per patient
Inappropriate use of antimicrobials (wrong dose, for non-bacterial infections) — a major driver of antimicrobial resistance
Over-use of injections where oral formulations would work
Prescribing that doesn’t follow clinical guidelines
Inappropriate self-medication, often with prescription-only drugs
Non-adherence to prescribed dosing regimens

Scale of the problem: WHO estimates more than half of all medicines worldwide are prescribed, dispensed, or sold inappropriately, and half of all patients fail to take them correctly.

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
Substandard and Falsified Medical Products
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
In 2017, the World Health Assembly retired the term “counterfeit medicines” in favour of Substandard and Falsified (SF) medical products:

Substandard — authorized medical products that fail to meet quality standards or specifications
Falsified — products that deliberately and fraudulently misrepresent their identity, composition, or source

Why the term changed: “counterfeit” is a legal/intellectual-property concept (trademark infringement) and doesn’t necessarily indicate a health risk. The new terms reframe the issue as a public health problem, separate from patent and trademark disputes.

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
Generic vs. Branded Medicines
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

Branded/innovator medicine — sold under a manufacturer’s trademark, often while under patent protection
Generic medicine — a bioequivalent copy of an approved medicine, sold under its chemical/generic name (or a different brand) once patent protection expires, typically at much lower cost

Generic substitution is one of the most effective, low-cost levers for improving access to essential medicines — most NLEM medicines are available generically.

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
Access to Medicines: Broader Determinants
🟣 MAY KNOW
Beyond the essential-medicines list itself, actual access depends on:

Rational selection and use (covered above)
Sustainable financing and affordable pricing
Reliable health and supply systems (procurement, storage, distribution — including cold-chain where needed)
Sound regulatory systems to keep substandard/falsified products out of the supply chain

These four pillars are the standard WHO framework for describing access to essential medicines as a health-system, not just a pharmacological, issue.

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
The 2017 SSFFC-to-SF Terminology Shift
🟣 MAY KNOW
Before 2017, WHO used the unwieldy acronym SSFFC (Substandard/Spurious/Falsely-labelled/Falsified/Counterfeit) medical products. This was simplified to SF (Substandard and Falsified) at the Seventieth World Health Assembly specifically to separate the public health question (is this medicine safe and effective?) from intellectual-property law (is this a trademark violation?) — two questions that had previously been conflated under one confusing label.

title: Module 6: Hospital-Acquired Infections
text:
Definition and Classification
🟢 MUST KNOW
A hospital-acquired (nosocomial) infection is one a patient develops during treatment for another condition, not present or incubating at admission — conventionally, onset after 48 hours of admission. It can also affect healthcare workers.
The four most common types, each linked to an invasive device or procedure:







Type
Simplified criterion




Urinary tract infection
Positive culture, ≥10⁵ bacteria/mL


Surgical site infection
Purulent discharge/abscess/cellulitis within a month of surgery


Respiratory infection (esp. ventilator-associated pneumonia)
Respiratory symptoms + new infiltrate or purulent sputum


Vascular catheter infection / septicaemia
Inflammation at insertion site, or fever + positive blood culture

title: Module 6: Hospital-Acquired Infections
text:
Source, Spread, and Recipient
🟢 MUST KNOW
HAIs are analyzed from three angles:

Source — other patients, hospital staff (Staph aureus commonly carried in nose/skin; Salmonella in the gut), or the environment itself (hospital dust, surfaces)
Route of spread — direct contact (most common: via hands), droplet, airborne particles, or contaminated equipment/procedures (catheterization, IV lines, dressings)
Recipient — all patients are potential recipients, but risk is highest in the seriously ill, those on corticosteroids, and patients in ICU, urology, geriatric, or special newborn care units

title: Module 6: Hospital-Acquired Infections
text:
Prevention: Standard Precautions
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Applied to the care of every patient, regardless of known infection status:

Hand hygiene — the single most important measure, since hands are the most common route of transmission; alcohol-based disinfectant when soap and water alone is insufficient
Personal protective equipment — gloves for any contact risking contamination; gown, mask, and eye protection where splashing is anticipated
Sharps handled with extreme care; hands washed immediately after glove removal
Isolation of infectious patients; susceptible patients kept away from infection sources
Dust and droplet control — wet dusting/vacuum cleaning (not dry sweeping), face masks, adequate bed spacing, ventilation

title: Module 6: Hospital-Acquired Infections
text:
Device-Specific Prevention
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Evidence-based measures differ by infection type — knowing what doesn’t work is as important as what does:








Infection
Proven effective
Proven NOT effective




UTI
Limiting catheter duration, aseptic insertion, closed drainage
Systemic antibiotic prophylaxis


Surgical site
Clean OR environment, optimal antibiotic timing, aseptic technique
Preoperative shaving, fumigation


Ventilator pneumonia
Aseptic suctioning, limiting ventilation duration
Routine ventilator-circuit changes every 48–72h


Vascular catheter
Closed system, limited duration, aseptic insertion
Antimicrobial skin creams

title: Module 6: Hospital-Acquired Infections
text:
Nursing and Administrative Measures
🟣 MAY KNOW








Approach
Focus
Purpose




Barrier nursing
PPE, isolation, dedicated equipment, strict hand hygiene protocols
Prevent infection spread


Task nursing
Each staff member repeats specific duties across all patients, supervised by a head nurse
Efficient care delivery



Administrative control: every hospital should have a Control of Infection Committee — responsible for policies on admission of infectious cases, isolation facilities, disinfection procedures, and overall HAI surveillance and response.

title: Module 4: Poliomyelitis
text:
Welcome
Poliomyelitis
Learning Objectives:

Describe poliovirus, its reservoir, and modes of transmission
Classify the clinical spectrum of polio infection
Recognize the features of paralytic poliomyelitis
Compare IPV and OPV — mechanism, advantages, and complications
Explain AFP surveillance and vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV)
Outline India’s path to polio-free certification

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

Polio is a landmark eradication success story — India was certified polio-free in 2014 after being one of the last endemic reservoirs. This module pairs the biology with the surveillance/vaccination programme that achieved that result.

title: Module 4: Poliomyelitis
text:
Agent, Reservoir, and Transmission
🟢 MUST KNOW
Agent: poliovirus (RNA virus), 3 serotypes — most paralytic outbreaks are type 1. Reservoir: humans only, no chronic carriers, no animal source. Most infections are subclinical — for every clinical case there may be ~1,000 subclinical infections in children, driving silent community spread.
Transmission: primarily faeco-oral (contaminated water, food, fingers, flies); droplet spread can occur during the acute phase and matters more where sanitation is already good.
Incubation period: 7–14 days (range 3–35 days). Most vulnerable age in India: 6 months–3 years.

title: Module 4: Poliomyelitis
text:
Clinical Spectrum
🟢 MUST KNOW
Only about 1% of infections involve the CNS and cause paralysis — the rest fall into three non-paralytic categories:







Form
Features




Inapparent (subclinical)
No symptoms; detected only by virus isolation or rising antibody titre


Abortive polio
Mild, self-limiting illness from viraemia; not clinically distinguishable without lab tests


Non-paralytic polio
Neck/back stiffness and pain, synonymous with aseptic meningitis; recovery in 2–10 days


Paralytic polio
Virus invades the CNS — see next slide

title: Module 4: Poliomyelitis
text:
Paralytic Polio: Recognition
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

Asymmetrical flaccid paralysis is the hallmark, preceded by fever at onset
Paralysis is descending (hip → distal limb), asymmetric and patchy, with proximal muscles more affected than distal
Progresses to its maximum in under 4 days (up to 4–7); deep tendon reflexes diminish before paralysis onset; no sensory loss
Bulbar/bulbospinal forms involve cranial nerves — facial asymmetry, swallowing difficulty; respiratory insufficiency is the usual cause of death

No specific treatment exists — management is supportive: good nursing care and early physiotherapy to minimize residual disability.

title: Module 4: Poliomyelitis
text:
IPV vs. OPV
🟡 SHOULD KNOW









IPV (Salk)
OPV (Sabin)




Type
Inactivated, injectable
Live attenuated, oral


Immunity induced
Humoral only (IgG/IgM/IgA in serum)
Humoral and intestinal (secretory IgA)


Herd effect
None — doesn’t block gut transmission
Strong — vaccine virus spreads to contacts, achieving herd immunity at ~66% coverage


Epidemic use
Poor fit — needs multiple doses, injections risky during outbreaks
Well suited — rapid, can interrupt transmission


Key risk
None significant
Rare Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Polio (VAPP), mostly linked to Sabin type 3



India’s routine schedule uses OPV (birth dose + primary series) with fractional-dose IPV (fIPV) introduced nationally after a 2016 VDPV2 detection — 2 intradermal fIPV doses achieve higher seroconversion than one full IM dose.

title: Module 4: Poliomyelitis
text:
AFP Surveillance
🟣 MAY KNOW
Since polio itself is often silent, Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) case reporting is the surveillance backbone — any child with sudden flaccid paralysis is investigated, whether or not polio is suspected clinically.

Sensitivity target: ≥1 non-polio AFP case per 100,000 children under 15 detected annually — proof the system is sensitive enough to catch a real case if one occurred
Two stool specimens, 24–48 hours apart, within 14 days of paralysis onset, shipped to a WHO-accredited lab within 72 hours
Environmental surveillance (testing sewage, e.g. in Mumbai) can detect circulating poliovirus even without a clinical AFP case

title: Module 4: Poliomyelitis
text:
Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus and India’s Eradication
🟣 MAY KNOW

VDPV — the live OPV strain, in communities with low vaccination coverage, can genetically revert over prolonged circulation and cause paralysis indistinguishable from wild-type polio; classified as circulating (cVDPV), immunodeficiency-associated (iVDPV), or ambiguous (aVDPV)
Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) — India’s mass campaign strategy since 1995: two immunization rounds 4–6 weeks apart, during the low-transmission season (Nov–Feb), targeting every child under 5 regardless of prior immunization status, as extra doses supplementing (not replacing) routine immunization

Outcome: India was certified polio-free on 27 March 2014. Wild poliovirus type 2 (eradicated 2015) and type 3 (eradicated 2019) are gone globally; type 1 is the only wild strain still circulating anywhere.

title: Module 2: Typhoid Fever and Cholera
text:
Welcome
Typhoid Fever and Cholera
Learning Objectives:

Identify the agent, reservoir, and carrier states of typhoid fever
Describe the clinical course, complications, and diagnosis of typhoid
Explain the pathogenesis and clinical stages of cholera
Compare oral and injectable typhoid vaccines
Outline cholera outbreak control, including rehydration therapy

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

Both diseases share a faeco-oral transmission route and the same core control principles (safe water, sanitation, food hygiene) already introduced in Chapter 6 — this module focuses on what’s specific to each.

title: Module 2: Typhoid Fever and Cholera
text:
Typhoid Fever: Agent and Reservoir
🟢 MUST KNOW
Agent: Salmonella typhi (main cause); S. paratyphi A/B less frequent. Survives intracellularly; killed by drying, pasteurization, common disinfectants.
Reservoir — humans only:

Cases — infectious as long as bacilli appear in stool/urine
Carriers — temporary (incubatory/convalescent) or chronic (excretes bacilli for over a year, often from the gall bladder/biliary tract; develops in 2–5% of cases). Famous example: “Typhoid Mary,” linked to over 1,300 cases as a lifelong chronic carrier

Transmission: faeco-oral / urine-oral, via contaminated water, food, fingers, and flies. Incubation period: 10–14 days (range 3 days–3 weeks).

title: Module 2: Typhoid Fever and Cholera
text:
Typhoid Fever: Clinical Course
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

Fever — classic “step-ladder” rise over 7–10 days, then plateau with a toxic, exhausted appearance
GI features — constipation or pea-soup (“khaki green”) diarrhoea, abdominal distension
Rose spots — pink, blanching papules on the trunk, appearing in week 2
Complications (up to 10%, mainly after 2 weeks untreated): intestinal haemorrhage (sudden temperature drop, blood in stool) and intestinal perforation (classically in week 3)

Case fatality: ~1% with early treatment vs. up to 10–20% untreated; mortality is roughly 10× higher in children under 4.

title: Module 2: Typhoid Fever and Cholera
text:
Typhoid Fever: Diagnosis and Control
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Diagnosis: blood culture is the mainstay (also bone marrow, stool). Widal test measures O and H antibodies (O appears day 6–8, H day 10–12) but has only moderate sensitivity/specificity and cross-reacts with other Salmonella — a negative Widal does not exclude typhoid.
Control of reservoir: early diagnosis, notification, isolation until stool/urine cultures are negative; chronic carriers treated with prolonged ampicillin/amoxicillin + probenecid, or cholecystectomy in refractory biliary carriage.
Vaccination: Vi polysaccharide (injectable, single dose, IM/SC, protection from day 7, revaccinate every 3 years) or Ty21a (oral, live-attenuated, 3-dose regimen on alternate days). Neither gives 100% protection but both reduce incidence and severity.

title: Module 2: Typhoid Fever and Cholera
text:
Cholera: Agent and Clinical Picture
🟢 MUST KNOW
Agent: Vibrio cholerae O1 (classical or El Tor biotype) or O139. Most infections are mild or asymptomatic; typical cases show sudden, profuse, painless, watery diarrhoea (“rice-water stools”) followed by vomiting, rapid dehydration, and muscle cramps.
Pathogenesis: the organism does not invade tissue — cholera toxin activates adenylate cyclase in gut epithelium, raising cAMP and driving massive fluid/electrolyte secretion into the lumen.
Without rapid rehydration, case fatality can reach 30–40% — this is almost entirely a disease of fluid loss, not tissue invasion.
Incubation period: a few hours to 5 days, commonly 1–2 days.

title: Module 2: Typhoid Fever and Cholera
text:
Cholera: Transmission and Diagnosis
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Transmission: faecally contaminated water (wells, ponds, rivers) and contaminated food/drink; gastric acidity is a key host defence — the vibrio is destroyed at pH ≤5, which is why achlorhydria and antacid use raise susceptibility.
Carriers: healthy persons excreting V. cholerae in stool; incubatory carriers are short-lived (short incubation period), but some convalescent/chronic carriage occurs.
Diagnosis: dark-field microscopy of fresh stool can give a rapid presumptive diagnosis (vibrios show characteristic “shooting star” motility); definitive diagnosis is stool culture on bile salt agar with slide agglutination (Inaba/Ogawa subtyping).

title: Module 2: Typhoid Fever and Cholera
text:
Cholera: Outbreak Control
🟣 MAY KNOW
Standard sequence once an outbreak is suspected (echoes Chapter 6’s general outbreak-investigation framework, applied to cholera):

Verify the diagnosis (stool culture for V. cholerae O1/O139)
Notify local/national health authorities
Active case-finding in the community
Establish accessible treatment centres — 90%+ of cases can be managed with oral rehydration alone; only severe dehydration needs IV fluids
Rehydration therapy (mortality reduced to <1% with effective rehydration)
Antibiotics as an adjunct only, once vomiting has stopped (fluoroquinolones, tetracycline, azithromycin)
Sanitation measures — safe water, excreta disposal, food hygiene, disinfection

Mass chemoprophylaxis is not recommended — treating ~10,000 people to prevent one serious case is not cost-effective and has repeatedly failed to stop spread. Oral cholera vaccines (e.g. Dukoral) exist but supplement, not replace, water/sanitation measures.

title: Selected Communicable Diseases
text:
Selected Communicable Diseases
Chapter 6 covers the general principles of communicable disease epidemiology — the chain of infection, transmission, herd immunity, and outbreak investigation. This section applies those principles to six specific diseases in depth, each as its own module.

Module 1: Malaria — agent, life cycle, clinical types, diagnosis, treatment, and NVBDCP

Module 5: Food Poisoning and Diarrhoeal Disease Control — bacterial agents, oral rehydration therapy, and India’s programme

title: Module 1: Malaria
text:
Welcome
Malaria
Learning Objectives:

Identify the agent, vector, and reservoir of malaria
Describe the parasite life cycle in man and mosquito
Distinguish the clinical types of malaria by species
Compare methods of diagnosis and outline treatment by species
State the key malariometric indicators used in surveillance
Describe India’s malaria control programme (NVBDCP) and strategy

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This module extends Chapter 6’s general communicable-disease principles (chain of infection, vector control) to malaria specifically — the first of several vector-borne and enteric diseases covered as dedicated modules.

title: Module 1: Malaria
text:
Agent, Reservoir, and Vector
🟢 MUST KNOW
Malaria is caused by four Plasmodium species, transmitted by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito:








Species
Share of cases
Note




P. vivax
~70%
Benign tertian; relapses (hypnozoites)


P. falciparum
~25–30%
Malignant tertian; responsible for severe/fatal malaria; no relapse


P. malariae
uncommon
Quartan fever (every 4th day)


P. ovale
rare
Mainly Africa; relapses



Reservoir: humans only — either a case (clinical malaria) or a carrier (asymptomatic gametocyte carriage; children more often carriers than adults).

title: Module 1: Malaria
text:
Life Cycle
🟢 MUST KNOW
The parasite completes its life cycle across two hosts:

In man (asexual cycle) — sporozoites injected by the mosquito bite reach the liver, multiply into schizonts, and release merozoites into the blood. Merozoites invade RBCs (erythrocytic phase); rupture of infected RBCs causes the fever paroxysm. P. vivax/ovale leave dormant hypnozoites in the liver → later relapse; P. falciparum does not relapse.
In the mosquito (sexual cycle / sporogony) — ingested gametocytes fertilize in the mosquito gut, forming an oocyst that produces sporozoites, which migrate to the salivary glands (10–20 days, temperature/humidity dependent) — the mosquito is now infective.

Incubation period: vivax ≈14 days · falciparum ≈12 days · malariae ≈28 days · ovale ≈17 days.

title: Module 1: Malaria
text:
Clinical Features
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Benign tertian (P. vivax): the classic three-stage paroxysm — cold stage (chills, rigors) → hot stage (103–104°F) → sweating stage — fever on alternate days; repeated attacks → splenomegaly, anaemia.
Malignant tertian (P. falciparum): continuous fever, classic stages often absent; can progress to cerebral malaria (convulsions, coma), blackwater fever (haemoglobinuria), or algid/septicaemic malaria (shock) — the life-threatening form.
Quartan (P. malariae): fever every 4th day. Ovale malaria: similar to vivax, mainly in Africa.

title: Module 1: Malaria
text:
Diagnosis
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
All suspected cases require parasitological confirmation:

Light microscopy — thick smear (detects presence/absence); thin smear (identifies species and parasite stage) — remains the gold standard
Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDTs) — immunochromatographic antigen detection, results in ~15 minutes; can distinguish P. falciparum from non-falciparum

Suspected case definition: fever in a person living in or having recently visited an endemic area during transmission season, with no other confirmed diagnosis.

title: Module 1: Malaria
text:
Treatment Principles
🟣 MAY KNOW

P. vivax — chloroquine (blood stages) plus primaquine for 14 days (clears liver hypnozoites, prevents relapse)
P. falciparum — Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT, e.g. artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine) plus a single dose of primaquine (gametocytocidal, blocks transmission)
Primaquine is contraindicated in pregnancy, infants, and G6PD deficiency (risk of haemolysis)
Mixed infections involving falciparum are treated as falciparum malaria
Pregnancy: ACT in the 2nd/3rd trimester for falciparum (quinine in the 1st trimester); chloroquine for vivax

title: Module 1: Malaria
text:
Malariometric Indicators
🟣 MAY KNOW
Used to measure transmission intensity and evaluate control programmes:

Annual Parasite Incidence (API) — confirmed cases per 1,000 population per year (India’s key programme metric)
Slide Positivity Rate (SPR) / Slide Falciparum Rate (SFR) — % of examined blood smears positive overall / positive for falciparum
Infant Parasite Rate — most sensitive indicator of active transmission; considered interrupted if zero for 3 consecutive years
Entomological indices — vector density, human blood index, sporozoite rate (vector-side transmission risk)

title: Module 1: Malaria
text:
NVBDCP and Malaria Elimination
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
India’s malaria programme has evolved considerably:
NMCP (1953) → NMEP (1958) → Modified Plan of Operation (1977) → National Anti-Malaria Programme (1999) → NVBDCP (2003–04) → National Framework for Malaria Elimination 2016–2030
Control strategy (three-pronged): early diagnosis and complete treatment (passive + active surveillance) · integrated vector control (indoor residual spray, ITNs/LLINs, source reduction) · behaviour change communication and community participation.
Vaccine: RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix®) — WHO-recommended since October 2021, the first licensed anti-parasite vaccine; effective against P. falciparum only, ~40% efficacy, 4-dose schedule from 5 months of age.
India’s progress: Annual Parasite Incidence fell from 2.09 (2000) to 0.13 (2022); malaria deaths fell from 932 to 83 over the same period.

title: Module 3: Viral Hepatitis
text:
Welcome
Viral Hepatitis
Learning Objectives:

Compare hepatitis A–E by transmission route, incubation, and chronicity
Interpret the HBV serological marker panel (HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBs)
Describe hepatitis B prevention: vaccine, HBIG, and passive-active immunization
Recognize hepatitis C’s shift to direct-acting antivirals
Identify why hepatitis E is especially dangerous in pregnancy

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

Five clinically distinct viruses cause “viral hepatitis” — this module organizes them by the single most useful axis for undergraduate exams: faeco-oral (A, E) vs. blood-borne/parenteral (B, C, D) transmission, since that axis predicts chronicity, prevention strategy, and severity in pregnancy.

title: Module 3: Viral Hepatitis
text:
Hepatitis A–E at a Glance
🟢 MUST KNOW










Type
Route
Incubation
Chronic state?
Vaccine




A
Faeco-oral
10–50 days
No
Yes (inactivated/live)


B
Parenteral, perinatal, sexual
30–180 days
Yes
Yes (recombinant)


C
Parenteral (blood)
2 weeks–6 months
Yes (55–85%)
No


D
Parenteral, requires HBV co-infection
Variable
Yes, if HBV chronic
Prevented via HBV vaccine


E
Faeco-oral (water)
3–8 weeks
Usually no (chronic only if immunosuppressed)
Yes (China only)



Exam pattern: A and E are faeco-oral, self-limiting, and never become chronic; B, C, and D are blood-borne and can become chronic — this single distinction predicts most of what differs in prevention and prognosis below.

title: Module 3: Viral Hepatitis
text:
Hepatitis B: Serological Markers
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
HBV has three antigen–antibody systems that together stage infection — classic MBBS exam material:

HBsAg (surface antigen, “Australia antigen”) — presence beyond 6 months defines the chronic carrier state
HBeAg — marker of active viral replication and higher infectivity
Anti-HBs — indicates immunity, either from past infection or vaccination
Anti-HBc (IgM) — marks recent/acute infection

High-risk groups: surgeons (~50× general-population incidence), transfusion recipients, healthcare/lab workers, infants of HBV-carrier mothers, and people who are immunocompromised — all recommended for screening and vaccination.

title: Module 3: Viral Hepatitis
text:
Hepatitis B: Prevention
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

Hepatitis B vaccine — recombinant (HBsAg-based), given IM in the deltoid (anterolateral thigh in infants); 3 doses at 0, 1, and 6 months; included in India’s pentavalent vaccine (DPT + Hep B + Hib)
Hepatitis B Immunoglobulin (HBIG) — passive immunization for acute exposure (needle-stick, newborn of a carrier mother); most effective within 6 hours, ideally not later than 48 hours
Passive-active immunization — HBIG + vaccine given together is more effective than either alone, and is the standard approach for a newborn of an HBsAg-positive mother

No specific curative treatment exists for hepatitis B — this is why prevention (vaccination, blood screening) is the primary public-health strategy.

title: Module 3: Viral Hepatitis
text:
Hepatitis C: A Changing Picture
🟣 MAY KNOW

Transmitted almost entirely via blood exposure (transfusion, needle-stick, injection drug use) — not through food, water, or casual contact
~80% of new infections are asymptomatic; of those infected, 55–85% develop chronic infection, with 15–30% cirrhosis risk over 20 years
Treatment has been transformed: older interferon + ribavirin regimens (48 weeks, ~50% cure, significant side effects) have been replaced by direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) — 12-week courses that cure most patients with far fewer adverse effects
No vaccine exists for hepatitis C — prevention relies entirely on blood safety and injection safety

title: Module 3: Viral Hepatitis
section: Hepatitis E: Special Risk in Pregnancy
text:
Hepatitis E: Special Risk in Pregnancy
🟣 MAY KNOW

A water-borne disease; genotype 1 (common in India and South Asia) causes community outbreaks, unlike genotype 3 (developed countries)
Usually self-limiting with complete recovery — except in pregnancy, where hepatitis E can cause fulminant hepatitis with a case fatality of up to 20% in the third trimester
No specific treatment; prevention relies on safe water and sanitation (the same measures already covered for cholera and typhoid)

Exam tip: hepatitis E is the one viral hepatitis where pregnancy itself is a major severity risk factor — this is the single fact most often tested.

title: Module 5: Food Poisoning and Diarrhoeal Disease Control
text:
Welcome
Food Poisoning and Diarrhoeal Disease Control
Learning Objectives:

Compare the major bacterial causes of food poisoning
Calculate ORS requirements and apply WHO rehydration guidelines
Distinguish cholera from shigella diarrhoea clinically
Explain the role of zinc supplementation in diarrhoea management
Identify key preventive strategies against diarrhoeal disease
Recognize amoebiasis and soil-transmitted helminths as related enteric threats

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This module closes the enteric-disease cluster (typhoid, cholera, hepatitis A/E, and now food poisoning) with the single most consequential intervention across all of them: oral rehydration therapy.

title: Module 5: Food Poisoning and Diarrhoeal Disease Control
text:
Bacterial Food Poisoning: A Comparison
🟢 MUST KNOW









Agent
Source
Incubation
Key feature




Staphylococcus aureus
Milk products (preformed enterotoxin)
1–6 hours
Rapid-onset vomiting, cramps


Salmonella
Meat, milk, eggs
12–24 hours
Fever, vomiting, diarrhoea


Bacillus cereus (emetic)
Fried rice, pasta (preformed toxin)
1–6 hours
Upper GI symptoms (vomiting)


Bacillus cereus (diarrhoeal)
Soup, gravy, meat
12–24 hours
Lower GI symptoms (diarrhoea)


Clostridium botulinum
Home-canned/preserved food
18–36 hours
Neurological: diplopia, dysphagia, weakness — can be fatal


Clostridium perfringens
Reheated meat/poultry
6–24 hours
Diarrhoea, cramps



Pattern to remember: a preformed toxin (Staph, B. cereus emetic form, botulism) gives fast onset within hours; an organism that must multiply and invade first (Salmonella, C. perfringens) takes longer.

title: Module 5: Food Poisoning and Diarrhoeal Disease Control
text:
Investigating a Food Poisoning Outbreak
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Standard steps, applying the general outbreak-investigation framework (Chapter 6) to a food-borne event:

History-taking — interview everyone who shared the food: what was eaten, when, symptom onset and type, in order of occurrence
Laboratory investigation — culture stool/vomit/food remnants; examine kitchen staff’s stool samples too
Food-specific attack rates — calculated for each food item to identify the culprit
Case-control study — used to statistically confirm the association between illness and a specific food

Prevention: meat inspection, food-handler personal hygiene (exclude those with wounds/diarrhoea from food handling), rapid cooling/cold storage, and thorough cooking (most agents killed above 60°C).

title: Module 5: Food Poisoning and Diarrhoeal Disease Control
text:
Oral Rehydration Therapy
🟢 MUST KNOW
The single most important intervention for acute watery diarrhoea:
ORS required (first 4 hours) = body weight (kg) × 75 mL/kg

Give as much ORS as the patient wants, monitoring for continued dehydration signs
Vomiting is not a reason to stop — wait 10 minutes, then resume slowly (a spoonful every 2–3 minutes)
Continue breastfeeding and normal feeding throughout — food should never be withheld or diluted; this is a major shift from older “starve the diarrhoea” practice

Maintenance therapy (after initial rehydration): oral fluid intake should match ongoing stool loss — roughly 10–15 mL/kg/hour for severe diarrhoea if stool volume can’t be measured directly.

title: Module 5: Food Poisoning and Diarrhoeal Disease Control
text:
Cholera vs. Shigella: Clinical Differentiation
🟡 SHOULD KNOW



Feature
Cholera
Shigella




Stool
Watery, “rice-water”
Bloody/mucoid


Fever
Absent
Present


Vomiting
Present
Absent


Rectal pain (tenesmus)
Absent
Present



Why it matters: antibiotics are indicated only when the cause is clearly identified (shigella, typhoid, cholera) — routine antibiotic use in undifferentiated diarrhoea causes more harm than benefit. Cholera: doxycycline/tetracycline. Shigella: ciprofloxacin (often resistant to ampicillin/TMP-SMX).

title: Module 5: Food Poisoning and Diarrhoeal Disease Control
text:
Zinc Supplementation and Prevention
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Zinc — WHO/UNICEF recommend 10 mg/day (under 6 months) or 20 mg/day (over 6 months) for 10–14 days during acute diarrhoea. This reduces episode duration/severity and lowers diarrhoea incidence for the following 2–3 months.
Broader prevention (better MCH care practices):

Breastfeeding promotion — breast-fed children have far lower severe-diarrhoea and death risk than bottle-fed children
Appropriate weaning — not too early (before 6 months) or too late, with hygienically prepared, nutritious foods
Vitamin A supplementation — reduces child mortality by 19–54%, substantially via reduced diarrhoeal and measles deaths
Rotavirus vaccine — included in India’s Universal Immunization Programme, targeting the leading viral cause of severe childhood diarrhoea

title: Module 5: Food Poisoning and Diarrhoeal Disease Control
text:
Amoebiasis and Soil-Transmitted Helminths
🟣 MAY KNOW
Two further faeco-orally transmitted enteric conditions worth recognizing alongside bacterial/viral diarrhoea:

Amoebiasis (Entamoeba histolytica) — faeco-oral transmission via contaminated water/food; ranges from asymptomatic cyst passage to amoebic dysentery and, rarely, liver abscess. Control mirrors typhoid and cholera: safe water, sanitation, food hygiene
Soil-transmitted helminths (STH) — roundworm (Ascaris), hookworm, whipworm; transmitted via soil contaminated by human faeces (eggs ingested, or hookworm larvae penetrate skin). Public health control relies on periodic deworming, sanitation, and footwear use
Guinea worm (dracunculiasis) — transmitted via contaminated drinking water containing infected copepods; a WHO-targeted eradication disease, controlled almost entirely through safe water and case containment rather than drugs

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Welcome
Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
Learning Objectives:

Describe the six links in the chain of infection
Distinguish endemic, sporadic, epidemic, and pandemic disease occurrence
Classify modes of transmission of communicable disease
Define basic reproduction number (R₀) and herd immunity threshold
Describe carrier states and why chronic carriers matter
Distinguish incubation period, generation time, and serial interval
Distinguish isolation from quarantine
Compare live, killed, toxoid, and subunit vaccines
Apply the levels of prevention to communicable disease control
Outline the standard steps of an outbreak investigation

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter applies Chapter 2’s levels of prevention and Chapter 3’s epidemiological triad specifically to infectious disease, and opens the Diseases section of the curriculum.

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
The Chain of Infection
🟢 MUST KNOW
Communicable disease transmission depends on six linked elements — break any one link, and transmission stops:

Infectious agent — the causative organism
Reservoir — where the agent lives and multiplies (human, animal, or environment)
Portal of exit — how the agent leaves the reservoir (respiratory tract, gut, skin, blood)
Mode of transmission — how it travels to a new host
Portal of entry — how it enters the new host
Susceptible host — an individual capable of being infected

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Epidemic, Endemic, and Pandemic
🟢 MUST KNOW
Disease occurrence is classified by how its frequency compares to what’s normally expected in a place and population:







Term
Meaning




Endemic
Constant, expected presence of a disease in a given area/population, without importation


Sporadic
Cases occur irregularly and infrequently, with no consistent pattern


Epidemic
Cases clearly in excess of normal expectancy for that place, population, and season


Pandemic
An epidemic spanning multiple countries/continents, usually affecting large numbers of people


Exotic
A disease imported into an area where it does not otherwise occur



Zoonoses — infections naturally transmissible between vertebrate animals and humans — are classified by direction: anthropozoonoses (animal → human, e.g. rabies, anthrax), zooanthroponoses (human → animal, e.g. human TB in cattle), and amphixenoses (either direction).

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Modes of Transmission
🟢 MUST KNOW


Direct transmission

Direct contact (touch, sexual contact)
Droplet spread (coughing, sneezing, over short distance)
Transplacental (mother to fetus)


Indirect transmission

Vehicle-borne — contaminated water, food, fomites
Vector-borne — via an insect/arthropod (mechanical or biological)
Airborne — droplet nuclei or dust suspended in air over distance

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Reservoirs of Infection
🟢 MUST KNOW

Human reservoir — a case (symptomatic) or a carrier (asymptomatic but infectious)
Animal reservoir — diseases transmitted from vertebrate animals to humans are called zoonoses
Environmental reservoir — soil, water (e.g. tetanus spores in soil, Legionella in water systems)

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Basic Reproduction Number (R₀)
🟢 MUST KNOW
R₀ is the average number of secondary infections produced by one infected person in a completely susceptible population.

R₀ > 1 → each case generates more than one new case → epidemic potential
R₀ < 1 → the outbreak is expected to die out
R₀ = 1 → disease remains endemic at a steady rate

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Herd Immunity
🟢 MUST KNOW
Herd immunity is indirect protection of susceptible individuals when a sufficiently high proportion of a population is immune, breaking chains of transmission even for those who aren’t immune themselves.
Herd immunity threshold (HIT):
HIT = 1 − (1 / R₀)
Example: a disease with R₀ = 3 needs roughly two-thirds (66%) of the population immune to interrupt sustained transmission.

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
section: Levels of Prevention Applied to Communicable Disease
text:
Levels of Prevention Applied to Communicable Disease
🟢 MUST KNOW
Chapter 2’s levels of prevention map directly onto infectious disease control:







Level
Communicable disease example




Primordial
Improving sanitation and housing before any outbreak risk exists


Primary
Immunization, vector control, safe water


Secondary
Case detection, contact tracing, early treatment


Tertiary
Rehabilitation from disease sequelae (e.g. post-polio care)

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Types of Vaccines
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Immunizing agents used for primary prevention fall into distinct categories, each with different implications for immunity and administration:








Type
How it works
Examples




Live attenuated
Weakened live organism; usually strong, long-lasting immunity from few doses
BCG, OPV, MMR


Killed / inactivated
Whole organism inactivated; safer in immunocompromised hosts, but needs boosters
Inactivated polio (IPV), rabies


Toxoid
Inactivated bacterial toxin, not the organism itself
Tetanus, diphtheria


Subunit / conjugate
Only a specific antigenic component, reducing side effects
Hepatitis B, Hib



Exam tip: live vaccines are generally contraindicated in pregnancy and immunocompromised individuals, since the attenuated organism can still replicate.

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Isolation vs. Quarantine
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

Isolation — separating a person already known to be infected (diagnosed or symptomatic) from others, until no longer contagious
Quarantine — separating a person who was exposed but is not yet known to be infected, for the duration of the incubation period, to see if disease develops

Both are control measures acting on different links of the chain of infection — isolation removes an active reservoir; quarantine interrupts transmission from a potential future case.

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Carrier States
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
A carrier is an infected person who sheds the agent without (or before/after) showing overt disease — carriers matter because they’re often missed by clinical surveillance.

By type: incubatory (sheds during incubation) · convalescent (continues shedding after clinical recovery, e.g. typhoid, cholera) · healthy (shedding without ever having overt disease, e.g. poliomyelitis)
By duration: temporary (short-lived shedding) vs. chronic (indefinite shedding — the greater public-health threat, since the longer the carrier state, the greater the cumulative community risk)

Why carriers matter more than cases, sometimes: a diagnosed case is usually isolated; an unrecognized chronic carrier keeps transmitting silently.

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Incubation Period and Related Intervals
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Incubation period — the time between exposure to an infectious agent and the first sign or symptom of disease. It depends on infective dose, portal of entry, and host susceptibility, and is used to set quarantine duration and trace likely sources.
Two related, easily confused intervals:

Generation time — from receipt of infection to that host’s own peak infectivity
Serial interval — the gap between symptom onset in a primary case and symptom onset in a secondary case it infects

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Secondary Attack Rate
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Secondary Attack Rate (SAR) measures how contagious a disease is within a close-contact group (e.g. a household), following exposure to a primary case:
SAR = (New cases among contacts) / (Total susceptible contacts)
Related concept — incubation period: the time between exposure to an infectious agent and the first appearance of symptoms; it determines how long quarantine should last.

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Outbreak Investigation: The 10 Steps
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
The standard CDC-style sequence for investigating a suspected outbreak:

Prepare for field work
Establish the existence of an outbreak
Verify the diagnosis
Define and identify cases
Describe data by time, place, and person
Develop hypotheses
Evaluate hypotheses
Refine hypotheses / conduct additional studies
Implement control and prevention measures
Communicate findings

(In practice these steps often overlap and don’t run strictly in order — control measures, for instance, are often started well before the investigation formally concludes.)

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Explore: Selected Diseases in Depth
🟣 MAY KNOW
The principles above apply to every communicable disease — six specific diseases are covered in dedicated modules, each with agent, clinical features, diagnosis, treatment, and control in full depth:
Malaria · Typhoid Fever & Cholera · Viral Hepatitis · Poliomyelitis · Food Poisoning & Diarrhoeal Disease · Hospital-Acquired Infections
Or browse the module hub for an overview of all six.

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Emerging and Re-emerging Infections
🟣 MAY KNOW

Emerging infectious diseases — newly identified, or newly significant, infections in a population (e.g. a novel pathogen)
Re-emerging infectious diseases — previously controlled diseases that increase again (e.g. due to declining vaccination coverage, antimicrobial resistance, or ecological change)

Both categories are driven by similar factors: urbanization, travel, climate change, land-use change, and breakdowns in public health infrastructure.

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Smallpox Eradication
🟣 MAY KNOW
Smallpox remains the only human disease ever declared eradicated (WHO, 1980), achieved through a global vaccination campaign combined with surveillance-containment (“ring vaccination” around each detected case) rather than mass vaccination alone. It remains the reference case study for what a successful global eradication program requires: an effective vaccine, no animal reservoir, and a recognizable, short-lived infectious stage.

title: Mental Health
text:
Welcome
Mental Health
Learning Objectives:

State the WHO definition of mental health
Recognize mental disorders as a major, under-addressed share of the global disease burden
Trace India’s National Mental Health Programme and District Mental Health Programme
Describe the Mental Healthcare Act 2017’s rights-based approach, including Section 115
Explain WHO’s mhGAP task-shifting strategy for closing the mental health treatment gap

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter closes the Diseases section by extending Chapter 1’s dimensions-of-health framework (physical, mental, social, …) into a full treatment of mental health as a public health priority in its own right, not an afterthought to physical disease.

title: Mental Health
text:
What Is Mental Health?
🟢 MUST KNOW
WHO definition: mental health is a state of mental well-being that enables people to cope with the stresses of life, realize their abilities, learn and work well, and contribute to their community.

Mental health has both intrinsic and instrumental value, and is recognized as a basic human right
It exists on a continuum, experienced differently by each person — directly echoing Chapter 2’s health–disease spectrum concept
A combination of individual, family, community, and structural factors can either protect or undermine it at any given time

title: Mental Health
text:
The Burden of Mental Disorders
🟢 MUST KNOW
Common mental disorders — depression, anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and substance use disorders — together contribute a very large share of the global burden of disease when measured in DALYs, because they are long-duration and disabling rather than usually immediately fatal (recall Chapter 7’s point about NCDs and disability).
Key structural problem — the treatment gap: in most countries, especially low- and middle-income ones, the majority of people with a diagnosable mental disorder never receive any formal treatment.

title: Mental Health
text:
National Mental Health Programme, India (1982)
🟢 MUST KNOW
India launched its National Mental Health Programme (NMHP) in August 1982, one of the first countries to do so at national scale, with three core objectives:

Ensure availability and accessibility of minimum mental healthcare for all, especially the most vulnerable and underprivileged
Encourage application of mental health knowledge in general healthcare and social development
Promote community participation in mental health service development

title: Mental Health
text:
District Mental Health Programme (DMHP)
🟢 MUST KNOW
Piloted in Bellary district, Karnataka (1985–1990) by NIMHANS — offering outpatient services, a small inpatient facility, referral services, education/awareness, and community screening — and formally added to the NMHP in 1996.
Significance: DMHP demonstrated that basic mental healthcare could be delivered through the general primary health care system, at the district and primary-health-centre level, rather than requiring specialized psychiatric hospitals alone — a direct application of the Alma-Ata primary health care principles from Chapter 1.

title: Mental Health
text:
Mental Healthcare Act, 2017
🟢 MUST KNOW
India’s Mental Healthcare Act (2017) shifted the legal framework toward a rights-based approach, including:

The right to access mental healthcare as a legal entitlement
Advance directives — a person can specify, in advance, how they wish (or don’t wish) to be treated during a future mental health crisis
Section 115 — a person who attempts suicide is presumed to be under severe stress unless proven otherwise, and shall not be tried or punished under the Indian Penal Code’s suicide-attempt provision; the state instead has a duty to provide care, treatment, and rehabilitation

Effect of Section 115: it doesn’t formally repeal the underlying IPC provision, but makes prosecution for a suicide attempt practically impossible, reframing it as a health issue rather than a crime.

title: Mental Health
section: WHO mhGAP: Closing the Treatment Gap
text:
WHO mhGAP: Closing the Treatment Gap
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
WHO’s Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP), launched in 2008, responds to the wide gap between mental health needs and available resources, especially in LMICs, through task-shifting/task-sharing:

Trains non-specialist health workers (general nurses, doctors, community health workers) to identify and manage common mental, neurological, and substance-use conditions
Uses standardized, evidence-based intervention guides so care doesn’t depend on scarce specialist psychiatrists alone

This is the mental-health-specific application of the same resource-constrained, primary-care-centred logic behind DMHP.

title: Mental Health
section: Stigma as a Public Health Barrier
text:
Stigma as a Public Health Barrier
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Stigma — negative attitudes and discriminatory behaviour toward people with mental illness — is one of the strongest barriers to seeking and receiving mental healthcare, operating at multiple levels:

Public stigma — societal prejudice and stereotyping
Self-stigma — internalized shame that discourages help-seeking
Structural stigma — discriminatory policies, laws, or institutional practices (which the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 explicitly tries to reduce)

title: Mental Health
section: Community Mental Health vs. Institutional Care
text:
Community Mental Health vs. Institutional Care
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Global mental health policy — including India’s DMHP model — has shifted away from long-term custodial care in isolated psychiatric institutions, toward community-based mental health services: outpatient clinics, primary-care integration, day-care centres, and family/community support — improving both access and the person’s ability to remain integrated in their community, consistent with the “social” dimension of health from Chapter 1.

title: Mental Health
section: Suicide as a Public Health Issue
text:
Suicide as a Public Health Issue
🟣 MAY KNOW
Suicide is treated in modern public health policy as a preventable public health outcome, not solely an individual or moral failing — reflected in the Mental Healthcare Act’s shift from criminalization to care. Prevention strategies span means restriction, crisis helplines, media reporting guidelines, and integrating suicide-risk screening into routine primary care.

title: Mental Health
section: Common Mental Disorders: A Brief Overview
text:
Common Mental Disorders: A Brief Overview
🟣 MAY KNOW

Depression — persistent low mood and loss of interest/pleasure, the single largest contributor to years lived with disability globally
Anxiety disorders — excessive fear or worry disproportionate to actual threat
Bipolar disorder — alternating episodes of depression and mania
Schizophrenia — a severe disorder involving distortions in thinking, perception, and behaviour
Substance use disorders — harmful or dependent use of alcohol or other psychoactive substances

title: Module 1: Diabetes Mellitus
text:
Welcome
Diabetes Mellitus
Learning Objectives:

Describe the burden of diabetes globally and in India
Identify the agent, host, and environmental risk factors for diabetes
Apply WHO diagnostic criteria using FPG, 2-hour PG, and HbA1c
Describe whom to screen and how
Outline the principles of lifestyle modification and pharmacological management

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This module extends Chapter 7’s general NCD framework (four shared behavioural risk factors, WHO STEPS, population vs. high-risk strategy) to diabetes specifically — the first of three dedicated disease modules. Detailed drug pharmacology (dosing, duration of action) is intentionally left to a pharmacology course — this module stays at the community medicine level: epidemiology, screening, diagnosis, and management principles.

title: Module 1: Diabetes Mellitus
text:
Definition, Types, and Burden
🟢 MUST KNOW
Diabetes mellitus is a heterogeneous syndrome of chronic hyperglycaemia from defective insulin secretion, action, or both, disturbing carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism — one of the four priority NCDs targeted globally.

Global prevalence: 8.5% (2014), projected to affect 6 in 10 people by 2040; nearly half of people with diabetes are unaware they have it
India: second-largest diabetic population worldwide (~73 million, 2017); urban prevalence rose from ~2% (1970s) to over 20% today, with rural areas fast catching up

title: Module 1: Diabetes Mellitus
text:
Risk Factors
🟢 MUST KNOW







Category
Examples




Agent
Beta-cell destruction (viral: rubella, mumps, coxsackie B4; autoimmune), genetic defects in insulin structure/function


Host
Age, obesity (strongest modifiable risk factor), genetics (~90% concordance in identical twins for type 2), family history


Environmental / behavioural
Physical inactivity, diet high in saturated fat and refined carbohydrate, smoking (elevated risk persists ~10 years after cessation)



Clinical features: many patients are asymptomatic; classic presentation includes polyuria, polydipsia, recurrent genital infections, and generalized pruritus — only about 1 in 5 people can recognize their own symptoms.

title: Module 1: Diabetes Mellitus
text:
Screening and Diagnosis
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Whom to screen: family history of diabetes, overweight/obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, sedentary lifestyle, history of gestational diabetes or macrosomic birth, cardiovascular disease.
WHO diagnostic criteria:




Normoglycaemia
Prediabetes
Diabetes




FPG (mg/dL)
<110
110–125 (IFG)
≥126


2-hour PG (mg/dL)
<140
140–199 (IGT)
≥200


HbA1c
<5.7%
5.7–6.4%
≥6.5%



Re-screen normoglycaemic individuals every 3 years; prediabetic individuals annually. OGTT uses a 75 g glucose load, with fasting and 2-hour samples.

title: Module 1: Diabetes Mellitus
text:
Management Principles
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Goals: glycaemic control, prevention of acute/chronic complications, symptom relief, managing comorbidities (obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia), and behavioural change support.
Lifestyle modification (first-line, all patients): diet (complex carbohydrates and fibre over refined sugar; limit saturated/trans fat), regular physical activity, tobacco cessation, stress management, and structured diabetes education on self-care and monitoring.
Pharmacological management (broad categories, by mechanism):

Oral hypoglycaemic agents — sulfonylureas (stimulate insulin secretion), biguanides/metformin (reduce hepatic glucose output; first choice in obese type 2 patients), and others targeting glucose absorption or post-prandial spikes
Insulin — required at diagnosis for symptomatic hyperglycaemia, ketosis, severe infection, or very high FPG/HbA1c; also used in pregnancy, acute stress states, and hepatic/renal failure

title: Module 3: Stroke
text:
Welcome
Stroke
Learning Objectives:

Describe the descriptive epidemiology of stroke
Identify major and other risk factors for stroke
Apply primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention to stroke
Explain why stroke mortality has declined in some countries

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

Stroke risk factors overlap heavily with coronary artery disease (CAD) and with hypertension (previous module) — this module emphasizes that overlap rather than treating stroke as an isolated condition.

title: Module 3: Stroke
text:
Descriptive Epidemiology
🟢 MUST KNOW
Stroke (cerebrovascular disease) — sudden loss of brain function due to a vascular lesion; a leading cause of death and a major source of disability and economic impact. Can occur in children, though with different risk factors than adult stroke.

Age: the strongest determinant — incidence roughly doubles each decade after age 55; mortality also rises with age
Sex: higher incidence in males
Time trend: a striking decline in stroke mortality in many countries, attributed mainly to better hypertension control, secondary prevention after TIA, reduced smoking, and improved acute treatment

title: Module 3: Stroke
text:
Risk Factors
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Stroke risk factors are largely shared with coronary artery disease — this overlap is the single most testable fact about stroke epidemiology:

Major: hypertension (the single most important risk factor), smoking, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes mellitus, heart disease, polycythaemia, thrombocythaemia
Other: family history, oral contraceptive use, previous stroke/TIA, carotid bruit, obesity, physical inactivity, high alcohol intake, drug abuse, trauma, coexisting CAD or peripheral vascular disease

title: Module 3: Stroke
text:
Prevention
🟢 MUST KNOW
Applying the standard levels-of-prevention framework (Chapter 2) to stroke specifically:







Level
Action




Primary
Detect and control risk factors — especially hypertension, smoking, hypercholesterolaemia, diabetes, heart disease, TIA


Secondary
Early detection (no definitive screening test exists; carotid bruit auscultation in high-risk individuals is reasonable); low-dose aspirin has a suggested but not firmly proven role


Tertiary
Acute treatment — rehabilitation, anticoagulants in selected cases; preventing recurrence — antiplatelet therapy, carotid endarterectomy in selected cases



Exam tip: unlike cancer or diabetes, stroke has no established population screening test — prevention relies almost entirely on controlling upstream risk factors (primary prevention), which is why hypertension control gets so much emphasis.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Welcome
Nutrition and Health
Learning Objectives:

Distinguish undernutrition, overnutrition, and the double burden of malnutrition
Compare kwashiorkor and marasmus as forms of protein-energy malnutrition
Define stunting, wasting, and underweight using WHO Z-score criteria
Name the major micronutrient deficiency disorders
Identify low birth weight and its major risk factors
Describe lathyrism as a food-toxin (not deficiency) disease
Outline India’s flagship nutrition programme structure (ICDS → POSHAN Abhiyaan → Saksham Anganwadi & Poshan 2.0)

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter connects the NCD chapter’s “double burden” language to nutrition specifically, and gives the anthropometric vocabulary (stunting/wasting/underweight) used throughout Indian public-health program monitoring.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Malnutrition: The Spectrum
🟢 MUST KNOW
Malnutrition covers deficiencies, excesses, or imbalances in a person’s intake of energy and/or nutrients — it is not only about “too little”:

Undernutrition — wasting, stunting, underweight, and micronutrient deficiencies
Overnutrition — overweight, obesity, and diet-related NCDs

Double burden of malnutrition: the coexistence of undernutrition and overnutrition — across a population, within the same household, and even within the same individual over their lifetime (e.g. a stunted child who later becomes an obese adult).

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Protein-Energy Malnutrition: Marasmus
🟢 MUST KNOW
Marasmus — PEM without edema — results from an overall calorie deficiency (inadequate intake of all nutrients, especially energy).
Clinical picture: severe muscle wasting, depletion of body fat, low weight-for-height, reduced mid-upper arm circumference, a head that looks disproportionately large, dry skin, thin hair, and irritability.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Protein-Energy Malnutrition: Kwashiorkor
🟢 MUST KNOW
Kwashiorkor — PEM with edema — results primarily from severe dietary protein deficiency, despite near-adequate energy (calorie) intake.
Clinical picture: peripheral pitting edema, “moon facies,” maintained or increased body fat, hepatomegaly, dry/peeling skin, and apathy.
A mixed form (marasmic-kwashiorkor), combining features of both, also occurs.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Anthropometric Indicators of Undernutrition
🟢 MUST KNOW
WHO Child Growth Standards classify undernutrition using Z-scores (standard deviations from the median of a healthy reference population), each below −2 SD:








Indicator
Reflects
Type




Stunting (low height-for-age)
Chronic undernutrition
Long-term


Wasting (low weight-for-height)
Acute undernutrition
Short-term


Underweight (low weight-for-age)
Both chronic and acute
Composite



Exam tip: underweight is a composite measure and can result from either stunting, wasting, or both — it doesn’t tell you which.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Major Micronutrient Deficiencies
🟢 MUST KNOW

Vitamin A deficiency — the leading cause of preventable childhood blindness (xerophthalmia); also increases infection mortality
Iron deficiency anaemia — the most common micronutrient deficiency globally, particularly affecting women and children
Iodine deficiency disorders (IDD) — ranging from goitre to irreversible cognitive impairment (cretinism) if deficient during pregnancy/infancy

Each has a dedicated national control program in India (Vitamin A Prophylaxis, National Iron Plus Initiative, National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme).
Two more diet-linked conditions worth knowing: endemic fluorosis from excess fluoride in drinking water (fully covered as a water-quality topic in Water Module 6), and food-borne illness from bacterial toxins or contamination (fully covered in Communicable Diseases Module 5) — both sit at the intersection of nutrition and environmental/communicable disease, so they’re treated in depth where they best fit rather than repeated here.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
India’s Nutrition Programme Architecture
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
India’s flagship child/maternal nutrition support has evolved through three stages:

ICDS (1975) — Integrated Child Development Services, India’s original flagship programme for children 0–6 years and pregnant/ lactating mothers, delivered through Anganwadi Centres
POSHAN Abhiyaan (2018) — India’s National Nutrition Mission; universalized and better-integrated ICDS with other nutrition schemes, aiming for measurable reductions in stunting, wasting, and anaemia
Saksham Anganwadi & Poshan 2.0 (2021–26) — the current umbrella scheme, merging ICDS, POSHAN Abhiyaan, the Scheme for Adolescent Girls, and the National Crèche Scheme into one integrated nutrition support programme

(Broader health-programme structures and financing are covered in Health Programmes in India.)

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Growth Monitoring
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Regular growth monitoring — plotting a child’s weight and height against standard growth charts over time — is a core Anganwadi/primary care activity, because:

It detects faltering growth early, before overt clinical malnutrition develops
It is a surveillance tool, not just an individual diagnostic one — aggregated data guide district- and state-level nutrition programming
It links directly to the iceberg phenomenon (Chapter 2): most undernutrition in a community is sub-clinical unless actively measured

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Undernutrition’s Long-Term Link to NCDs
🟣 MAY KNOW
WHO notes that undernutrition early in life — including in utero — may predispose a person to overweight and non-communicable diseases like diabetes and heart disease later in life (the “fetal origins” or Barker hypothesis). This is part of why the double burden of malnutrition is described as occurring across an individual’s life course, not only across a population at one point in time.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Body Mass Index (BMI)
🟣 MAY KNOW
For adults, nutritional status is commonly screened using Body Mass Index (BMI) = weight (kg) / height² (m²), with WHO cutoffs of underweight (<18.5), normal (18.5–24.9), overweight (25–29.9), and obese (≥30) — though these cutoffs are population-level screening tools, not a substitute for individual clinical assessment.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
text:
Welcome to Module 1
One Health Framework
Learning Objectives:

Define One Health and understand its three interconnected pillars
Explain the relevance of One Health to water contamination and public health
Describe India’s National One Health Mission and its strategic goals
Analyze the One Health Index for India and state-level performance
Integrate WASH (Water, Sanitation, Hygiene) principles within One Health
Apply One Health principles to surveillance and disease prevention


This module introduces the foundational One Health concept, critical for understanding environmental health challenges, particularly water-related issues. The integration of human, animal, and environmental health is essential for addressing complex public health problems.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
text:
What is One Health?


Definition:
One Health is a collaborative, multisectoral, and transdisciplinary approach working at local, regional, national, and global levels with the goal of achieving optimal health outcomes.
Core Recognition:
The health of people is closely connected to the health of animals and our shared environment.




One Health Triad showing interconnection between Human Health, Animal Health, and Environmental Health


Source: U.S. Geological Survey, 2024


U.S. Government Definition established in 2017. The approach recognizes that approximately 60% of emerging infectious diseases in humans are zoonotic, originating from animals. Environmental factors like water quality directly impact both human and animal health.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
text:
The One Health Triad
Three Interconnected Pillars
1. Human Health - Disease surveillance and control - Public health infrastructure - Healthcare systems - Epidemiological monitoring
2. Animal Health - Veterinary services - Livestock management - Wildlife health monitoring - Zoonotic disease tracking
3. Environmental Health - Water quality and sanitation - Air pollution control - Soil health - Ecosystem biodiversity

Each pillar affects and is affected by the others. For example, antimicrobial use in livestock (Animal Health) can contaminate water sources (Environmental Health), leading to antimicrobial resistance affecting humans (Human Health).

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
section: Why One Health Matters for Water
text:
Why One Health Matters for Water
The Water-Health Nexus
Water as a Critical Interface:

Pathogen Transmission: Waterborne zoonotic diseases (leptospirosis, schistosomiasis)
Chemical Contamination: Agricultural runoff (nitrates, pesticides) from animal farming
Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR): Antibiotics from animal waste entering water systems
Environmental Reservoirs: Water bodies as habitats for disease vectors (mosquitoes, snails)

One Health Application:
Water contamination requires integrated solutions addressing human practices (sanitation), animal management (waste disposal), and environmental protection (watershed management).

Example: Nitrate contamination in groundwater results from excessive use of animal manure and chemical fertilizers (agriculture/animal health), contaminates drinking water (environmental health), and causes methemoglobinemia in infants (human health). This exemplifies the One Health interconnection.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
text:
Zoonotic Pathogens in Water
The Hidden Threat
Major Waterborne Zoonotic Diseases:









Disease
Pathogen

Transmission Route




Leptospirosis
Leptospira bacteria

Schistosomiasis
Schistosoma

Freshwater contact



One Health Surveillance: Monitoring water sources for both human and animal pathogens provides early warning of disease outbreaks.

Leptospirosis outbreaks in India often follow monsoon flooding when rat urine contaminates floodwaters. One Health approach requires coordinated rodent control, sanitation improvement, and public health awareness.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
text:
Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) in Water
A Growing Crisis
The AMR-Water Connection:

Source: 75-90% of antibiotics administered to livestock are excreted unchanged
Pathway: Animal waste → manure → agricultural runoff → surface/groundwater
Impact: Resistant bacteria and resistance genes contaminate drinking water sources

Consequences:

Human Health: Infections become harder to treat
Animal Health: Reduced efficacy of veterinary antibiotics
Environmental Health: Disruption of aquatic microbial ecosystems

One Health Solution: Integrated approach to regulate antibiotic use in humans, animals, and agriculture while improving wastewater treatment.

India is one of the world’s largest consumers of antibiotics in livestock production. Studies have detected resistance genes in rivers, lakes, and even treated drinking water. The One Health approach mandates coordinated action across healthcare, veterinary services, and environmental sectors.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
text:
India’s National One Health Mission
Vision and Goals
Vision Statement: “To build an integrated disease control and pandemic preparedness system in India by bringing human, animal and environmental sectors together for better health outcomes, improved productivity and conservation of biodiversity.”
Initiated: Based on PM-STIAC’s (Prime Minister’s Science, Technology & Innovation Advisory Council) recommendation
Lead Agencies: - Ministry of Health & Family Welfare (MoHFW) - Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change (MoEFCC) - Department of Animal Husbandry & Dairying (DAHD) - AYUSH, DHR, DBT, NCDC, DRDO
Source: ICMR National One Health Mission, 2024

The mission represents India’s commitment to collaborative health security. It addresses gaps in existing One Health activities and coordinates previously siloed efforts across ministries.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
section: Six Focus Areas of India’s One Health Mission
text:
Six Focus Areas of India’s One Health Mission
Strategic Priorities
1. Zoonotic Disease Surveillance - Integrated disease surveillance at human-animal-environment interface - Early detection of emerging pathogens
2. Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) Control - Regulate antimicrobial use across sectors - Surveillance of resistance patterns
3. Food Safety - Farm-to-fork safety measures - Quality assurance of animal-origin foods
4. Laboratory Capacity Building - BSL-3/4 laboratory network for high-risk pathogens - Capacity for rapid outbreak response
5. Environmental Health Monitoring - Water quality surveillance - Air pollution and vector control
6. Research & Development - Vaccine platforms and diagnostics - Novel pathogen discovery using AI, NGS, metagenomics

Each focus area requires cross-sector collaboration. Environmental health monitoring, particularly water quality surveillance, is central to preventing disease transmission at the human-animal-environment interface.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
text:
One Health Mission: Key Initiatives
Implementation Strategies
Governance Structure:

Executive Steering Committee: Chaired by Health & Family Welfare Minister
Scientific Steering Committee: Led by Principal Scientific Advisor
Cross-Sector Coordination: Representation from all stakeholder ministries

Budget Allocation: ₹386.86 crore for disease control, R&D, and global collaboration
Key Programs:

BSL-3/4 Lab Network: National network for investigating emerging pathogens
Integrated Surveillance: Technology-enabled monitoring across habitats
Pandemic Preparedness: Under PM-ABHIM (Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission)
Digital Integration: AI and GIS-based zoonotic surveillance platforms

Source: PMF IAS, National One Health Mission Report, 2024

The mission integrates with existing programs like Swachh Bharat Mission (sanitation), JalJeevan Mission (safe water), and National Animal Disease Control Program, demonstrating comprehensive One Health implementation.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
text:
One Health Index for India
Measuring Performance
What is the One Health Index?
A composite metric assessing state-level capacity and performance across 13 key indicators related to human, animal, and environmental health integration.
13 Key Indicators Include:

Zoonotic disease surveillance infrastructure
Laboratory diagnostic capacity (BSL-2/3 labs)
Veterinary public health workforce
Water quality monitoring systems
AMR surveillance programs
Inter-sectoral coordination mechanisms
Environmental health regulations
Wildlife health monitoring
Food safety systems
Outbreak response capacity
Research & innovation output
Community awareness programs
Data sharing & integration platforms

Source: One Health Index Calculator for India (ICMR, 2024)

The index helps identify gaps and prioritize resource allocation across states. It enables evidence-based policymaking and tracks progress toward One Health goals.

Kerala’s top ranking reflects its strong public health systems, high literacy, effective surveillance, and inter-sectoral coordination. States like Bihar and UP face challenges in basic infrastructure, requiring targeted One Health investments.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
text:
WASH + One Health Integration
Water, Sanitation, Hygiene under One Health
Why WASH is Central to One Health:
WASH interventions prevent disease transmission across the human-animal-environment interface:

Safe Water: Prevents waterborne zoonoses (leptospirosis, cryptosporidiosis)
Sanitation: Breaks fecal-oral transmission of pathogens from humans and animals
Hygiene: Reduces direct contact with animal reservoirs and contaminated surfaces

One Health WASH Framework:

Integrated Water Quality Monitoring: Test for human AND animal pathogens
Livestock Waste Management: Prevent contamination of water sources
Community Hygiene: Educate on zoonotic disease prevention
Environmental Sanitation: Protect ecosystems supporting disease vectors

Source: PLOS Water Journal, “Towards a One Health approach to WASH”, 2024

Traditional WASH programs focus on human health. One Health WASH expands this to include animal health (veterinary WASH) and environmental health (ecosystem protection), recognizing that 80% of rural households in India live with livestock.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
section: Water Quality Surveillance: A One Health Application
text:
Water Quality Surveillance: A One Health Application
Integrated Monitoring Systems
Conventional Approach: - Monitor water for human pathogens only (E. coli, coliforms) - Reactive response after disease outbreaks
One Health Approach: - Monitor for human, animal, and environmental health indicators - Proactive surveillance for early warning
Example: Wastewater-Based Epidemiology (WBE)
# One Health Surveillance Data Integration
surveillance_data <- data.frame(
  Indicator = c("E. coli", "Leptospira", "Antibiotic Residues", 
                "Cryptosporidium", "Nitrate Levels"),
  Human_Health = c("High", "Medium", "High", "High", "High"),
  Animal_Health = c("Medium", "High", "High", "High", "Medium"),
  Env_Health = c("Medium", "Medium", "High", "Low", "High")
)
Application: COVID-19 wastewater surveillance detected viral RNA before clinical cases emerged, demonstrating the power of environmental monitoring for human disease.

Wastewater surveillance is a quintessential One Health tool. It monitors human pathogens (COVID, polio), animal pathogens (avian influenza), and environmental contaminants (AMR genes, heavy metals) simultaneously, providing early warning for public health interventions.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
section: Case Study: Cholera Outbreaks and One Health
text:
Case Study: Cholera Outbreaks and One Health
The Human-Animal-Environment Nexus
Background: Cholera (Vibrio cholerae) outbreaks in India often correlate with monsoon flooding and contaminated water sources.
One Health Analysis:







Component
Contributing Factors




Human
Poor sanitation, open defecation, crowded slums


Animal
Aquatic reservoirs (fish, shellfish), livestock near water sources


Environment
Flooding, water stagnation, temperature rise, algal blooms



One Health Interventions:

Human: Oral rehydration therapy, vaccination campaigns, hygiene education
Animal: Monitor aquatic animal health, regulate fish farming practices
Environment: Improve drainage, protect water sources, climate adaptation

Outcome: Integrated approach reduces cholera incidence by 60-70% compared to single-sector interventions.

The 2010 Haiti cholera outbreak demonstrated the consequences of ignoring the environment pillar. Contaminated river water (environmental failure) mixed with poor sanitation (human failure) caused a massive epidemic. One Health demands simultaneous action across all three sectors.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
section: One Health in Climate Change Context
text:
One Health in Climate Change Context
Emerging Challenges
Climate-Water-Health Linkages:

Extreme Weather: Floods contaminate water sources, droughts concentrate pathogens
Temperature Rise: Expands vector habitats (mosquitoes, snails) in water bodies
Altered Rainfall: Disrupts seasonal water availability, increases contamination
Ecosystem Disruption: Changes animal migration patterns, spreads diseases

One Health Climate Adaptation:
# Climate-sensitive disease forecasting model
climate_factors = {
    'temperature': 'increases vector breeding',
    'rainfall': 'floods lead to waterborne disease outbreaks',
    'humidity': 'affects pathogen survival in water',
    'extreme_events': 'infrastructure damage → sanitation failure'
}
India-Specific Impacts: - Increased dengue/malaria in previously non-endemic areas - More frequent waterborne disease outbreaks post-floods - Climate refugees migrating to areas with poor WASH infrastructure

Climate change is a threat multiplier for One Health. India experienced record floods in 2023-2024, leading to major waterborne disease outbreaks. One Health preparedness requires climate-resilient WASH infrastructure and early warning systems linking meteorological and epidemiological data.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
text:
Module 1 Summary
Key Takeaways
