title: Man and Medicine
text:
Welcome
Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All
Learning Objectives:

Define health and describe its dimensions and the health–disease spectrum
Explain the major determinants of health using an accepted health-field model
State the Alma-Ata Declaration’s definition of Primary Health Care and its goal
Trace the evolution of medicine from curative to community medicine
Describe the Bhore Committee’s role in shaping India’s health system
Locate “Health for All” within the later MDG → SDG trajectory

How to read this deck: each slide is tagged and color-coded — 🟢 MUST KNOW (core, exam-critical), 🟡 SHOULD KNOW (important context), 🟣 MAY KNOW (enrichment), and 🧡 QUESTION (self-check).

This chapter opens the Foundations section. It sets up vocabulary and frameworks — the definition of health, its determinants, and Primary Health Care — that every later chapter in this series assumes.
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
What Is Health?
🟢 MUST KNOW
WHO Constitution (1948):

“Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.”

This definition has never been formally amended. Two things make it radical for its time:

It rejects the purely biomedical view (health = absence of disease)
It names three dimensions at once — physical, mental, social — as jointly necessary


Drafted at the International Health Conference, New York, 1946; the WHO Constitution entered into force on 7 April 1948 (now marked annually as World Health Day).
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
Dimensions of Health
🟢 MUST KNOW


Commonly taught dimensions:

Physical — normal structure and function of the body
Mental — a state of balance with oneself and one’s environment
Social — harmony with the social fabric: family, community, work
Spiritual — a sense of purpose, values, or belief
Emotional — the ability to recognize and appropriately express feelings


Why this matters:
A person can be free of diagnosable disease and still not be “healthy” by this definition — e.g. someone who is physically fit but socially isolated or under chronic mental distress.
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
The Health–Disease Spectrum
🟢 MUST KNOW
Health is not a fixed state but a continuum, moving in both directions:
Death → Chronic illness → Disability → Mild sickness → No obvious illness → Positive health

Positive health is more than “not sick” — it implies resilience and a reserve capacity to cope with physical, biological, and social stress
Any individual can move along this spectrum over time; public health aims to shift populations toward the positive-health end, not just treat people once they’ve crossed into illness
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
Determinants of Health
🟢 MUST KNOW
A widely used health-field model groups the determinants of health into four domains:







Domain
Examples




Environment
safe water, sanitation, housing, air quality, occupational hazards


Heredity / Biology
genetic makeup, age, sex, inherited susceptibility to disease


Lifestyle / Behaviour
diet, physical activity, tobacco/alcohol use, personal hygiene


Health services
access, affordability, and quality of preventive and curative care



Key implication: health care services are only one of four determinants — and historically not the largest one. Improving population health depends at least as much on environment, behaviour, and social conditions as on hospitals and doctors.

This is the Blum / Lalonde-style “health field concept,” standard across Indian community-medicine teaching. Different sources add socio-economic and political factors as a fifth domain — mention this as a natural extension in discussion, not a contradiction.
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
Primary Health Care: Alma-Ata, 1978
🟢 MUST KNOW
At Alma-Ata (in present-day Kazakhstan), 134 WHO member states and 67 organisations adopted a declaration defining Primary Health Care (PHC):

“Essential health care based on practical, scientifically sound and socially acceptable methods and technology, made universally accessible to individuals and families… through their full participation and at a cost the community and country can afford… the first level of contact of individuals, the family and community with the national health system.”

The goal it set: “Health for All by the year 2000” — a level of health that would let all people lead a socially and economically productive life, with PHC declared the key strategy to reach it.
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
Principles of Primary Health Care
🟢 MUST KNOW

Equitable distribution — care reaches rural and underserved populations, not just cities
Community participation — individuals and communities help plan and run their own care, not just receive it
Intersectoral coordination — health links to agriculture, education, housing, water supply, and rural development
Appropriate technology — methods that are scientifically valid, affordable, and acceptable to the community, not merely the most advanced available
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
Evolution of Medicine
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Medicine’s scope has widened in stages:

Curative medicine — treating disease in the individual patient
Preventive medicine — stopping disease before it starts (e.g. immunization, screening)
Social medicine — recognizing that disease has social causes and consequences, not only biological ones
Community medicine / Public health — shifting the unit of concern from the individual patient to the community as a whole

Each stage didn’t replace the one before it — modern health systems practice all four simultaneously, for different needs.
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
The Bhore Committee (1946)
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
The Health Survey and Development Committee, chaired by Sir Joseph Bhore, was appointed by the colonial government in 1943 and reported in 1946. It remains the foundational blueprint for independent India’s health system.
Key recommendations:

Integrate preventive and curative services at every administrative level, instead of running them separately
Establish Primary Health Centres — short-term target of one PHC per 40,000 population
Strengthen maternal and child health services
Reorient medical education toward training “social physicians” — doctors trained in preventive and social medicine, not curative care alone
Raise health spending to at least 15% of government expenditure

Many of these ideas — the PHC network, integration of services — are still the structural basis of India’s public health system today.
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
section: From Health for All to the SDGs
text:
From Health for All to the SDGs
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
“Health for All by 2000” was not fully achieved by its target year, but it set a template that later global goals built on:

2000–2015: Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) — several goals (child mortality, maternal health, HIV/malaria/TB) were direct descendants of the Health for All agenda
2015–2030: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) — health consolidated under SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, with Universal Health Coverage (UHC) as an explicit target

(The MDG → SDG transition is covered in depth in Millennium Development Goals to SDGs; this slide only places it on the timeline.)
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
India’s National Health Policy Milestones
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

NHP 1983 — first National Health Policy; reaffirmed Health for All through a PHC-centred approach
NHP 2002 — revised targets in light of slower-than-planned progress; emphasized decentralization and public–private partnership
NHP 2017 — shifted emphasis toward Universal Health Coverage, preventive and promotive care, and raising public health spending as a share of GDP
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
A Longer View of Medicine
🟣 MAY KNOW

Hippocrates (Ancient Greece, c. 460–370 BCE) — separated medicine from religion and superstition; the source of the Hippocratic Oath’s ethical tradition
Sushruta (Ancient India) — author of the Sushruta Samhita, an early foundational text of surgery and Ayurvedic medicine
Public-health thinking is not a modern invention: sanitation and water-management systems appear in ancient urban civilisations (e.g. the Indus Valley), long before “public health” was named as a field
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
The Social Gradient of Health
🟣 MAY KNOW
Health outcomes follow a gradient across socioeconomic position, not just a gap between “poor” and “rich”: at every step up the social ladder, average health tends to improve. This is associated with the work of Michael Marmot and the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health.
Implication: improving population health requires acting on the “causes of the causes” — income, education, working conditions — not only on medical risk factors.
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Welcome
Screening for Disease
Learning Objectives:

Define screening and distinguish it from diagnosis
State the Wilson and Jungner criteria for a screening program
Calculate and interpret sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV
Describe the main types of screening
Explain lead time bias, length time bias, and overdiagnosis

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter closes the Foundations section by applying the incidence/ prevalence and 2x2-table thinking from Chapters 3–4 to the specific problem of evaluating a screening test and a screening program.

title: Screening for Disease
text:
What Is Screening?
🟢 MUST KNOW
Screening is the presumptive identification of unrecognized disease in apparently healthy, asymptomatic individuals, using tests that can be applied rapidly and economically to a large population.
Screening is NOT diagnosis:

A screening test sorts people into “likely disease” vs. “unlikely disease” — it does not confirm disease
Everyone who screens positive must still undergo a proper diagnostic test to confirm or rule out the condition

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Wilson and Jungner Criteria (1968)
🟢 MUST KNOW
WHO’s ten classic principles for deciding whether a condition is suitable for a screening program:

The condition should be an important health problem
There should be an accepted treatment for recognized disease
Facilities for diagnosis and treatment should be available
There should be a recognizable latent or early symptomatic stage
There should be a suitable test for that early stage
The test should be acceptable to the population
The natural history of the condition should be adequately understood
There should be an agreed policy on whom to treat
The cost of case-finding should be economically balanced against overall medical care spending
Case-finding should be a continuing process, not a one-time project

title: Screening for Disease
text:
The Screening 2×2 Table
🟢 MUST KNOW
Every screening test is judged against a reference/gold-standard diagnosis:




Disease +
Disease −




Test +
True Positive (TP)
False Positive (FP)


Test −
False Negative (FN)
True Negative (TN)



All four validity measures on the next slides come directly from this table.

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Sensitivity and Specificity
🟢 MUST KNOW
Sensitivity — the ability to correctly identify people who have the disease:
Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN)
Specificity — the ability to correctly identify people who do not have the disease:
Specificity = TN / (TN + FP)
Key property: both are properties of the test itself and do not depend on how common the disease is (prevalence) in the population tested.

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Predictive Values
🟢 MUST KNOW
Positive Predictive Value (PPV) — given a positive test, the probability the person actually has disease:
PPV = TP / (TP + FP)
Negative Predictive Value (NPV) — given a negative test, the probability the person is actually disease-free:
NPV = TN / (TN + FN)
Key property: unlike sensitivity/specificity, PPV and NPV do depend on disease prevalence — the same test will have a lower PPV in a low-prevalence population, even with unchanged sensitivity/specificity.

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Types of Screening
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

Mass screening — offered to an entire population, regardless of individual risk (e.g. a national program)
Selective/targeted screening — offered only to a high-risk subgroup (e.g. screening smokers for lung disease)
Multiphasic screening — several screening tests applied together in one session (e.g. a health camp offering blood pressure, blood sugar, and vision checks together)
Opportunistic screening — offered to a person who is already seeking care for an unrelated reason

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Lead Time Bias
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Lead time is the interval between detection by screening and the point when the disease would normally have been diagnosed clinically (from symptoms).
Lead time bias occurs when screening appears to prolong survival — because the clock on “survival” starts earlier — even if the person dies at exactly the same actual time as they would have without screening.
Why it matters: raw survival-time comparisons between screened and unscreened groups can be misleading unless lead time is accounted for.

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Length Time Bias and Overdiagnosis
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Length time bias — screening preferentially detects slow-growing, less aggressive disease, because it is present and detectable for longer; fast-growing, aggressive disease is more likely to cause symptoms and be diagnosed clinically between screening rounds. This makes screened cases look like they have better outcomes, independent of any real benefit.
Overdiagnosis — the extreme case: screening detects a genuine abnormality that would never have caused symptoms or harm in the person’s lifetime, leading to unnecessary labeling and treatment.

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Sensitivity–Specificity Trade-off
🟣 MAY KNOW
For a test with a continuous or graded result (e.g. a blood level), the cutoff chosen to define “positive” trades sensitivity against specificity: lowering the cutoff to catch more true cases (higher sensitivity) also increases false positives (lower specificity), and vice versa. This trade-off is often visualized with a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve, used to choose an optimal cutoff.

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Choosing Between Screening Designs
🟣 MAY KNOW
Mass screening is efficient for a common, serious, and well-understood condition (e.g. blood pressure), but wasteful and potentially harmful (overdiagnosis, false positives, anxiety) for rare conditions — reinforcing why the Wilson–Jungner criteria (importance, natural history, economic balance) matter before launching a program, not just whether a test technically exists.

title: Communication for Health Education
text:
Welcome
Communication for Health Education
Learning Objectives:

Describe the basic sender-message-channel-receiver-feedback communication model
Distinguish IEC from BCC
List and apply the six components of the Health Belief Model
Compare individual, group, and mass approaches to health education
Explain why one-way information provision is often insufficient for behaviour change

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter is the theory behind why health messaging (immunization uptake, sanitation behaviour, NCD risk-factor reduction) succeeds or fails, connecting back to nearly every earlier chapter’s programmes.

title: Communication for Health Education
text:
The Basic Communication Process
🟢 MUST KNOW
Every act of health communication involves the same core elements:

Sender — initiates and encodes the message
Message — the content being communicated
Channel — the medium carrying it (spoken, written, visual, electronic)
Receiver — decodes and interprets the message
Feedback — the receiver’s response, allowing the sender to confirm or correct how the message landed
Noise — anything that distorts or interferes with the message along the way (language barriers, distraction, competing beliefs)

Key principle: communication is a cycle, not a one-shot transmission — feedback is what makes it two-way.

title: Communication for Health Education
text:
IEC vs. BCC
🟢 MUST KNOW

IEC (Information, Education, Communication) — provides factual information and explains why it matters, largely as a one-way broadcast (posters, radio spots, pamphlets), on the assumption that informed people will act on what they learn
BCC (Behaviour Change Communication) — recognizes that information alone is often not enough; works as a two-way, dialogic process that also addresses real-world barriers to change, grounded in behavioural theory (like the Health Belief Model below)

The shift IEC → BCC mirrors the shift from a purely biomedical view of health communication to one that treats behaviour as shaped by more than knowledge alone — the same broader lesson as Chapter 1’s shift from a biomedical to holistic definition of health.

title: Communication for Health Education
text:
The Health Belief Model
🟢 MUST KNOW
A widely used framework explaining why people do or don’t take a health action, built on six components:

Perceived susceptibility — “Could this happen to me?”
Perceived severity — “How serious would it be if it did?”
Perceived benefits — “Would taking action actually help?”
Perceived barriers — “What’s stopping me / what would it cost me?”
Cues to action — a trigger prompting the behaviour (a symptom, a media campaign, a provider’s advice)
Self-efficacy — confidence in one’s own ability to actually carry out the action

Practical use: designing an effective health message means addressing more than one of these components at once — e.g. a message raising perceived severity without also raising self-efficacy can simply produce anxiety without behaviour change.

title: Communication for Health Education
text:
Methods of Health Education
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Health education is delivered through three broad approaches, each with different reach and depth trade-offs:

Individual approach — one-on-one counselling (highest depth/ personalization, lowest reach — e.g. a provider counselling a patient)
Group approach — group discussions, demonstrations, or health camps (moderate reach and depth — e.g. an Anganwadi nutrition demonstration)
Mass approach — radio, television, social media, posters (highest reach, lowest personalization — used for broad awareness campaigns)

No single method suits every goal — awareness campaigns favour mass approaches; sustained behaviour change (BCC) usually needs individual or group-level engagement as well.

title: Communication for Health Education
text:
Why Information Alone Often Fails
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Purely IEC-style, one-way messaging tends to underperform when:

Perceived barriers are structural, not just informational (e.g. cost, distance, social stigma) — no amount of awareness removes a real practical obstacle
Self-efficacy is low — people may believe an action is beneficial but doubt their own ability to sustain it
The message conflicts with existing cultural or social norms — addressed further in the next chapter’s discussion of medicine and social sciences

This is the core rationale for BCC’s more dialogic, barrier-addressing approach over pure information broadcast.

title: Communication for Health Education
text:
Social and Behaviour Change Communication (SBCC)
🟣 MAY KNOW
More recent practice has evolved IEC/BCC further into Social and Behaviour Change Communication (SBCC) — explicitly incorporating social and community-level influences (norms, peer networks, community leaders) alongside individual-level behaviour-change theory, rather than treating health communication as only an individual-level psychological process.

title: Communication for Health Education
text:
Communication Models: Transmission vs. Transactional
🟣 MAY KNOW
Communication theory distinguishes a simple transmission model (sender → message → receiver, largely one-way) from a transactional model, where sender and receiver continuously exchange and adapt roles in real time — the theoretical basis for why effective health education, especially BCC, functions best as an ongoing dialogue rather than a scripted broadcast.

title: Health Planning and Management
text:
Welcome
Health Planning and Management
Learning Objectives:

Describe the steps of the health planning cycle
Explain the criteria used for setting health priorities
Trace the role of India’s Five-Year Plans in health sector development, and the transition to NITI Aayog
List Gulick’s seven POSDCORB management functions
Apply the planning cycle to a national health programme example

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter is the operational/administrative counterpart to earlier programme-content chapters (11-15) — it explains how such programmes are planned and managed, not what they contain.

title: Health Planning and Management
text:
The Health Planning Cycle
🟢 MUST KNOW
A standard sequence used to plan any health programme or policy:

Situation analysis — collect and interpret data on the population, morbidity/mortality, disease distribution, existing facilities and manpower, and community attitudes and beliefs
Establishing objectives and goals
Assessing available resources
Fixing priorities
Writing up the formulated plan
Programming and implementation — translating policy into annual operational plans
Monitoring — ongoing tracking, enabling timely correction
Evaluation — assessing whether objectives were achieved (efficiency, acceptance, adequacy)

Note the direct parallel to Chapter 3’s descriptive epidemiology — situation analysis is essentially applying the person/place/time framework at the planning stage.

title: Health Planning and Management
text:
Setting Health Priorities
🟢 MUST KNOW
With finite resources, not every identified problem can be addressed at once. Standard criteria for prioritization include:

Burden of disease (DALYs — Chapter 21)
Equity — impact on the most disadvantaged groups (Chapter 23’s social determinants lens)
Feasibility — technical and political practicality of intervening
Cost-effectiveness — health gain per unit of resource spent

This is the planning-level application of Rose’s population vs. high-risk strategy trade-off from Chapter 7 — priority-setting decides which problems get a population-wide response at all.

title: Health Planning and Management
text:
India’s Five-Year Plans and Health
🟢 MUST KNOW
India ran twelve Five-Year Plans (1951–2017), formulated by the Planning Commission (established 1950, chaired by the Prime Minister), each setting specific economic and social development targets — including health-sector allocations for infrastructure, disease control, and human resources.

1969 — the Gadgil formula introduced transparent, criteria- based resource allocation to states
2015 — the Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India), which since the 12th Plan’s completion (2017) has taken over health-sector planning and programming with a more flexible, non-five-year framework

title: Health Planning and Management
text:
POSDCORB: Core Management Functions
🟢 MUST KNOW
Luther Gulick’s classic 1937 framework, describing the seven universal functions of any executive/manager — directly applicable to running a health programme or facility:

Planning
Organizing
Staffing
Directing
COordinating
Reporting
Budgeting

Why it’s still taught: it gives a simple, complete checklist for “what does managing a health programme actually involve” beyond just clinical or technical content — the same operational lens this chapter applies to Chapters 11–15’s programme content.

title: Health Planning and Management
section: Applying the Cycle: A Worked Example
text:
Applying the Cycle: A Worked Example
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Consider NSCAEM (Chapter 15): situation analysis established the disproportionate tribal-population sickle cell burden; priority setting targeted it specifically because of its concentrated, genetic, identifiable nature; implementation rolled out mass screening; monitoring tracks screening numbers against the 7-crore target; final evaluation will assess progress toward the 2047 elimination goal. Every named national programme in this curriculum has moved through these same planning-cycle stages, whether or not it’s stated explicitly.

title: Health Planning and Management
text:
Health Systems Building Blocks
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
WHO describes six interacting “building blocks” that any functioning health system’s planning must account for: service delivery, health workforce, health information systems, access to essential medicines, financing, and leadership/governance. Weakness in any one block — e.g. a health workforce shortage in tribal areas (Chapter 15) — limits the effectiveness of planning and management improvements made elsewhere.

title: Health Planning and Management
section: From Five-Year Plans to Flexible Governance
text:
From Five-Year Plans to Flexible Governance
🟣 MAY KNOW
The shift from fixed Five-Year Plans to NITI Aayog’s more continuous, flexible planning approach reflects a broader governance trend also seen in global health policy — the same broad movement from the MDGs’ fixed, time-bound targets to the SDGs’ more integrated, continuously monitored agenda (Chapter 12).

title: Health Planning and Management
text:
Management Span of Control
🟣 MAY KNOW
Gulick and Urwick, alongside POSDCORB, also argued for a limited “span of control” — recommending roughly 3–6 subordinates per manager for effective coordination — a principle still referenced in designing supervisory structures for large-scale health programmes with many frontline workers (e.g. ASHA supervision structures under NHM).

title: Medicine and Social Sciences
text:
Welcome
Medicine and Social Sciences
Learning Objectives:

Explain Talcott Parsons’s sick role concept, its rights and obligations
Define illness behaviour and its five components
Describe how culture shapes health-seeking behaviour
State the WHO Social Determinants of Health framework’s structural vs. intermediary determinants
Connect this chapter’s sociology/anthropology lens to earlier chapters’ health-education and prevention content

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter gives the sociological and anthropological theory underlying why health education (Ch17) and prevention programmes don’t work the same way for every population — behaviour is socially and culturally situated, not just individually rational.

title: Medicine and Social Sciences
text:
The Sick Role (Talcott Parsons)
🟢 MUST KNOW
Parsons (1950s) described illness as a state of “sanctioned deviance” — because a sick person isn’t a fully productive member of society, society grants them a recognized sick role, with defined rights and obligations:
Rights:

Exemption from normal social responsibilities (work, school)
Not being blamed for their condition

Obligations:

To see being sick as undesirable, and want to get well
To seek technically competent help (a doctor) once illness persists
To cooperate with treatment/medical advice

Why it matters: it frames illness as a social role, not just a biological state — connecting directly back to Chapter 2’s distinction between disease, illness, and sickness.

title: Medicine and Social Sciences
text:
Illness Behaviour
🟢 MUST KNOW
Health-seeking behaviour — any activity undertaken by a person who perceives themselves to have a health problem, aimed at finding an appropriate remedy. It has five recognized components:

Symptom definition — recognizing something is wrong
Illness-related shifts in role behaviour — adjusting daily activities in response
Lay consultation and referral — discussing symptoms with family/ community before (or instead of) a formal provider
Treatment actions — choosing a source of care (biomedical, traditional, or both)
Adherence — following through with the chosen treatment

Key insight: none of these steps are purely medical decisions — each is shaped by social and cultural context.

title: Medicine and Social Sciences
text:
Culture and Health-Seeking Behaviour
🟢 MUST KNOW
How people define illness, interpret symptoms, and decide where to seek care is shaped by cultural belief systems — including:

Spiritual/supernatural explanatory models of illness causation
Trust (or distrust) in the indigenous/traditional medical system versus the formal biomedical system
Perceived quality of communication with health professionals
Social norms around who is expected to seek care, and when

Direct link to Chapter 22: this is exactly why pure IEC-style messaging often fails — a message that ignores the target population’s explanatory model of illness is unlikely to change behaviour, however factually accurate it is.

title: Medicine and Social Sciences
section: WHO Social Determinants of Health Framework
text:
WHO Social Determinants of Health Framework
🟢 MUST KNOW
WHO defines social determinants of health as “the circumstances in which people are born, grow, work, live, and age, and the wider set of forces and systems shaping the conditions of daily life.”
The framework distinguishes two levels:

Structural determinants — the socioeconomic/political context that distributes power and resources unequally (governance, economic policy, education systems, social class, gender, ethnicity)
Intermediary determinants — the more immediate, everyday living/ working conditions this produces (employment conditions, housing, material circumstances)

Guiding principle: health equity — the absence of unfair and avoidable health differences between groups — directly extending Chapter 7’s discussion of the social gradient of health.

title: Medicine and Social Sciences
text:
Medical Sociology vs. Medical Anthropology
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

Medical sociology — studies how social structures, institutions, and roles (like the sick role) shape health, illness, and the practice of medicine within a society
Medical anthropology — studies how culture — beliefs, meanings, and practices — shapes how illness is experienced, explained, and treated across different societies

Both disciplines inform community medicine’s core premise: health cannot be understood purely biomedically, echoing the WHO definition of health from Chapter 1.

title: Medicine and Social Sciences
text:
Explanatory Models of Illness
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Every patient (and every provider) carries an explanatory model — a set of beliefs about what caused their illness, why it started when it did, what it does to the body, and what treatment should look like. Mismatched explanatory models between patient and provider — not lack of information — are a common, underappreciated cause of poor treatment adherence and dissatisfaction with care.

title: Medicine and Social Sciences
section: Stigma Revisited Through a Sociological Lens
text:
Stigma Revisited Through a Sociological Lens
🟣 MAY KNOW
Chapter 10 introduced stigma as a barrier to mental healthcare; medical sociology frames stigma more generally as a social process of labeling and devaluation applied to certain illnesses or conditions — applicable well beyond mental health, to conditions like leprosy, HIV/ AIDS, and tuberculosis, where the social consequences of a diagnosis can outweigh its clinical severity in shaping a person’s behaviour.

title: Medicine and Social Sciences
text:
Community-Based Participatory Approaches
🟣 MAY KNOW
Recognizing that social and cultural context shapes health behaviour has practically influenced programme design — favouring approaches that involve the community itself in defining problems and designing interventions (echoing Alma-Ata’s community-participation principle from Chapter 1), rather than externally designed programmes imposed without local input.

title: Demography and Family Planning
text:
Welcome
Demography and Family Planning
Learning Objectives:

Describe the four stages of the demographic transition model
Define and distinguish CBR, CDR, TFR, GRR, and NRR
Explain replacement-level fertility
Trace the history of India’s family planning programme, 1952 to present
State the goal of India’s National Population Policy 2000

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter gives the demographic vocabulary that underlies population- level health planning, and traces India’s role as a pioneer in national family planning policy.

title: Demography and Family Planning
text:
The Demographic Transition Model
🟢 MUST KNOW
A generalized description of how birth rates, death rates, and population growth change as a society moves from pre-industrial to industrialized, in four stages:

Stage 1 — High birth rate, high death rate → slow/stable growth (pre-industrial)
Stage 2 — Death rate falls (better sanitation/medicine), birth rate stays high → rapid population growth
Stage 3 — Birth rate begins to fall (urbanization, education, contraception) → growth slows
Stage 4 — Low birth rate, low death rate → stable population

Where most transitions stall or reverse today: some countries now describe a Stage 5, where birth rate falls below death rate, causing population decline — not part of the classical four-stage model but increasingly relevant.

title: Demography and Family Planning
section: Crude Birth Rate and Crude Death Rate
text:
Crude Birth Rate and Crude Death Rate
🟢 MUST KNOW
Crude Birth Rate (CBR) — live births per 1,000 mid-year population in a given year.
Crude Death Rate (CDR) — deaths per 1,000 mid-year population in a given year.
Both are “crude” because they don’t adjust for the population’s age or sex structure — a country with an older population will show a higher CDR even with excellent health care, simply due to demographics.

title: Demography and Family Planning
text:
Total Fertility Rate
🟢 MUST KNOW
Total Fertility Rate (TFR) — the average number of children a woman would bear over her lifetime, if she experienced the current age-specific fertility rates throughout her childbearing years.
Replacement-level fertility — the TFR at which a population exactly replaces itself across generations (approximately 2.1 in most settings, accounting for child mortality and the sex ratio at birth). A country with TFR consistently below this level will eventually see its population decline, absent migration.

title: Demography and Family Planning
text:
Gross and Net Reproduction Rate
🟢 MUST KNOW

Gross Reproduction Rate (GRR) — like TFR, but counts only daughters a woman would have — a measure of generational replacement through the female line, ignoring mortality
Net Reproduction Rate (NRR) — refines GRR further by also adjusting for the probability that daughters survive to their mother’s childbearing age; NRR = 1 means the population is exactly replacing itself generation to generation

Exam tip: GRR ignores mortality; NRR accounts for it — this is the key distinguishing feature between the two.

title: Demography and Family Planning
text:
India’s Family Planning Programme: Origins
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
In 1952, India became the first country in the world to launch an official national family planning programme, aiming to reduce birth rates “to stabilize the population at a level consistent with the requirements of the national economy.”

1966 — a separate Department of Family Planning created within the Ministry of Health
1977 — following the coercive sterilization controversies of the Emergency period, the new government’s population policy explicitly ruled out compulsion, making the programme purely voluntary — a landmark and lasting policy shift

title: Demography and Family Planning
text:
National Population Policy 2000
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
India’s National Population Policy (NPP) 2000 set its goals around:

Addressing unmet need for contraception
Providing free and compulsory school education up to age 14
Reducing infant and maternal mortality
Achieving population stabilization by 2045

NPP 2000 implementation was later integrated with the National Rural Health Mission (launched 2005) as the operational vehicle for delivering its goals, connecting demography policy directly to the health-systems architecture from Chapter 11.

title: Demography and Family Planning
section: Age Structure and the Population Pyramid
text:
Age Structure and the Population Pyramid
🟣 MAY KNOW
A population pyramid — a bar chart of population by age and sex — visually reflects a country’s demographic-transition stage: a wide base (many young people) indicates high fertility (early transition), while a more rectangular shape indicates low fertility and an ageing population (late transition). India’s own age structure varies significantly by state, reflecting different transition stages within one country.

title: Demography and Family Planning
text:
Demographic Dividend
🟣 MAY KNOW
The demographic dividend is the potential economic growth benefit that can arise when a country’s working-age population (15–64) is proportionally larger than its dependent population (children and elderly) — typically occurring during the middle stages of the demographic transition, as fertility falls but before the population ages substantially. Realizing this dividend depends on adequate education, employment, and health investment during that window.

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
Welcome
Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
Learning Objectives:

List the 8 Millennium Development Goals and identify the three explicitly health-focused ones
State the key SDG 3 health targets
Explain why the global development agenda moved from MDGs to SDGs
Distinguish the scope and design philosophy of the two frameworks

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

Chapter 1 already placed “Health for All” on the MDG->SDG timeline, and Chapter 7 already introduced SDG 3.4 in the NCD context. This chapter gives the full picture both of those referenced without repeating either.
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
The Eight Millennium Development Goals (2000–2015)
🟢 MUST KNOW

Eradicate extreme poverty and hunger
Achieve universal primary education
Promote gender equality and empower women
Reduce child mortality
Improve maternal health
Combat HIV/AIDS, malaria, and other diseases
Ensure environmental sustainability
Develop a global partnership for development

Three goals were explicitly health-focused: Goals 4, 5, and 6 — though several others (poverty/hunger, environment, global partnership) were also tracked using health-related indicators.
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
Key MDG Health Targets
🟢 MUST KNOW

Goal 4 (child mortality): reduce the under-five mortality rate by two-thirds between 1990 and 2015
Goal 6 (HIV/AIDS, malaria, other diseases): halt and begin to reverse the spread of HIV/AIDS by 2015; achieve universal access to HIV treatment by 2010; halt and begin to reverse malaria and other major diseases by 2015

Result: the MDGs galvanized unprecedented global attention, funding, and accountability on this focused set of concerns, with substantial — though incomplete — progress by 2015.
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
The Seventeen Sustainable Development Goals (2015–2030)
🟢 MUST KNOW
Adopted by all UN member states in September 2015, the SDGs comprise 17 goals and 169 targets, applying universally to all countries (not only low- and middle-income countries, as the MDGs largely did).
Health sits at SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being — “ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages” — with 13 targets covering a much broader spectrum than the three MDG health goals.
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
Key SDG 3 Targets
🟢 MUST KNOW

Maternal mortality: reduce the global ratio to below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030
Child mortality: end preventable newborn/under-5 deaths — targets of ≤12 neonatal deaths per 1,000 and ≤25 under-5 deaths per 1,000 live births
Communicable disease: end the epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, and neglected tropical diseases, and combat hepatitis and water-borne disease
SDG 3.4: reduce premature NCD mortality by one-third, and promote mental health (introduced already in the NCD chapter)
Universal Health Coverage (UHC) and access to safe, effective medicines and vaccines for all
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
Why the Agenda Broadened
🟡 SHOULD KNOW









MDGs
SDGs




Scope
8 goals, narrowly focused
17 goals, 169 targets, broad


Applies to
Primarily developing countries
Universally, all countries


Process
Perceived as top-down (set by experts/UN)
Developed through inclusive, participatory consultation


Health coverage
3 goals: child, maternal, infectious disease
1 goal (SDG 3), but covering both communicable AND non-communicable disease, injuries, and UHC



The shift reflects a recognition that health outcomes depend on interlocking sectors (poverty, education, environment, inequality) — consistent with the multifactorial-causation and social-determinants ideas from earlier chapters.
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
Criticism of the SDG Approach
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
The SDGs’ breadth is also their most common criticism: with 17 goals and 169 targets, analysts argue the framework is less focused and harder to measure than the MDGs, risking diffused attention and resources across too many priorities at once — a direct trade-off against the MDGs’ narrower, more trackable design.
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
The Paradigm-Shift Challenges
🟣 MAY KNOW
Achieving the SDG 3 health agenda has been described as requiring a genuine paradigm shift across five challenges: intersectoral leadership on the structural drivers of health, shifting focus from treatment to prevention, addressing commercial determinants of ill-health (e.g. tobacco, alcohol, ultra-processed food industries), integrating rights-based approaches, and strengthening civic engagement and accountability.
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
India’s MDG-to-SDG Transition
🟣 MAY KNOW
India, alongside other countries, undertook a formal national consultation process on transitioning its own monitoring and planning systems from MDG to SDG indicators — reflecting that the SDGs, unlike the MDGs, require every country (not only lower-income ones) to track and report progress against the same global framework.

This chapter closes Phase 3 by applying the social-determinants and double-burden-of-disease concepts from earlier chapters to a specific, policy-relevant Indian population group.

title: Tribal Health in India
section: Health Determinants Specific to Tribal Populations
text:
Health Determinants Specific to Tribal Populations
🟢 MUST KNOW
India’s Scheduled Tribes (Adivasi communities) — about 8.6% of India’s population — face a distinct combination of health determinants:

Geographic isolation — habitations scattered across large areas with poor connectivity, transport, and communication
Socio-economic disadvantage — disproportionately represented in the poorest wealth deciles
Undernutrition and anaemia — prevailing at higher rates than the general population (Chapter 9’s malnutrition framework applies directly here)
Genetic disorders — notably sickle cell disease and G-6-PD deficiency, concentrated in specific tribal populations due to historical patterns of inheritance and marriage within communities

title: Tribal Health in India
text:
Sickle Cell Disease Burden
🟢 MUST KNOW
Sickle cell disease is disproportionately concentrated in India’s tribal population:

Roughly 73% of Indians carrying the sickle haemoglobin gene (HbS) are from tribal communities — despite tribes being only ~8.6% of the population
Prevalence of the sickle cell trait/disease varies widely by region and community (roughly 1–40% trait prevalence in different populations)
Highest burden concentrated in states including Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, and Assam

Why this matters for prevention: because carrier/disease status can be identified through a simple test, sickle cell disease is a strong candidate for secondary prevention (early detection) at population scale (Chapter 2’s levels of prevention).

title: Tribal Health in India
section: National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (NSCAEM)
text:
National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (NSCAEM)
🟢 MUST KNOW
Announced in the 2023–24 Union Budget and launched by the Prime Minister on 1 July 2023 at Shahdol, Madhya Pradesh:

Goal: eliminate sickle cell disease as a public health problem in India by 2047
Target: universal screening of 7 crore (70 million) people aged 0–40 in affected tribal areas
Provides awareness generation, counselling, and access to affordable, quality care for those diagnosed — through collaboration between central ministries and state governments

This is a direct, named example of a vertical, disease-specific programme (Chapter 11’s terminology) targeted precisely because of the population-specific genetic burden described above.

title: Tribal Health in India
text:
Healthcare Infrastructure Gaps
🟢 MUST KNOW
Public health infrastructure in tribal regions is documented to be inadequate, understaffed, and underutilized, with a nationwide shortfall (relative to population-based norms) of thousands of Health Sub-Centres, Primary Health Centres, and Community Health Centres in tribal areas specifically.
Consequence: even where national programmes (NHM, Ayushman Bharat, NSCAEM) exist on paper, their reach into tribal areas is constrained by this underlying infrastructure gap — a reminder that programme design (Chapter 11) and programme reach are separate problems.

title: Tribal Health in India
text:
Expert Committee on Tribal Health
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
A four-year study led by Dr. Abhay Bang produced India’s first comprehensive tribal health report, “Tribal Health in India — Bridging the Gap and a Roadmap for the Future,” examining health status, cultural context, and healthcare infrastructure in tribal areas.
Key recommendation theme: addressing the underlying social determinants of tribal health (poverty, education, resource access) is as important as expanding clinical service delivery alone — echoing the social-determinants framing from Chapter 7’s discussion of the social gradient of health.

title: Tribal Health in India
text:
Access Barriers Beyond Infrastructure
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
The 2014 Xaxa Commission report identified additional non- infrastructure barriers specific to tribal communities:

Geographical isolation tied to remote/traditional living patterns
Lack of awareness of available health services
Cultural norms and beliefs that may not align with mainstream health-system practices, requiring culturally sensitive outreach rather than a one-size-fits-all delivery model

title: Tribal Health in India
text:
Digital-First Screening at Scale
🟣 MAY KNOW
NSCAEM has been noted for a digital-first approach — using digital tools to track screening, testing, and follow-up for a screening programme covering tens of millions of people across geographically dispersed and hard-to-reach tribal areas — an operational adaptation specifically shaped by the geographic-isolation challenge described earlier.

title: Tribal Health in India
text:
Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs)
🟣 MAY KNOW
Within India’s broader Scheduled Tribe population, the government designates certain groups as Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) — communities with pre-agricultural technology, low literacy, declining or stagnant population, and greater isolation than tribal populations generally — requiring even more targeted policy attention than the general tribal-health framework.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Low Birth Weight
🟢 MUST KNOW
Low Birth Weight (LBW) — birth weight under 2,500 g, regardless of gestational age; affected ~19% of Indian births.

Major risk factor: maternal malnutrition and anaemia
Other causes: heavy physical labour during pregnancy, maternal illness (especially infections)
Associated factors: short maternal stature, very young maternal age, high parity, smoking, closely spaced births

Why it matters: LBW is one of the strongest single predictors of infant mortality and later childhood undernutrition — prevention therefore centres on maternal nutrition and antenatal care rather than newborn intervention alone.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Lathyrism
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
A crippling food-toxin disease, distinct from a deficiency disease — caused by excess consumption rather than lack of a nutrient.

Cause: the neurotoxin BOAA (beta-oxalyl amino alanine) in Lathyrus sativus (khesari dal), when it makes up over 30% of the diet for 2–6 months
Neurolathyrism (humans) — gradually progressive spastic paralysis of the lower limbs, typically in adults aged 15–45; progresses through recognized stages (latent → no-stick → one-stick → two-stick → crawler) as muscular stiffness worsens
Reversibility: only in the earliest (latent) stage — removing the pulse from the diet at that point can produce complete remission; established paralysis in later stages is permanent

Control: banning cultivation in endemic areas, detoxification (steeping/parboiling the pulse before use), and health education — essentially the same primary-prevention logic as any other diet-attributable disease, just aimed at removing a harmful food rather than adding a deficient nutrient.

title: Occupational Health
text:
Lead Poisoning
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
A classic occupational heavy-metal toxicity, from lead smelting, battery manufacture, printing, and paint work.

Absorption: inhalation of lead dust/fumes (main occupational route) and ingestion (contaminated hands/food)
Clinical picture: anaemia (basophilic stippling of RBCs), abdominal colic, peripheral neuropathy (classically wrist drop), and a blue-black “lead line” on the gums
Prevention: substitution of lead-free materials where possible, engineering controls (exhaust ventilation, enclosed processes), personal hygiene (no eating in the work area), and periodic blood-lead monitoring
Management: removal from exposure plus chelation therapy in confirmed toxicity

title: Occupational Health
text:
Occupational Cancers
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Certain workplace exposures are established carcinogens — occupational cancer is one of the few cancer categories where the causative exposure is often precisely identifiable:







Cancer
Occupational exposure




Skin cancer
Tar, soot, mineral oils, arsenic, UV/ionizing radiation


Lung cancer
Asbestos, arsenic, chromium, nickel, radon (mining)


Bladder cancer
Aromatic amines (dye, rubber, and printing industries)


Leukaemia
Benzene and ionizing radiation



Control of industrial cancer follows the same levels-of-prevention logic as any occupational disease: substitution of the carcinogen where possible, engineering controls to limit exposure, and periodic medical surveillance for early detection in exposed workers.

title: Occupational Health
text:
Occupational Dermatitis and Agricultural Hazards
🟣 MAY KNOW
Occupational dermatitis — the most common occupational skin condition, from repeated contact with irritants (solvents, cement, oils) or allergens (nickel, rubber chemicals); prevention relies on protective clothing/gloves and skin barrier creams rather than treatment alone.
Agricultural workers face a distinct hazard profile from industrial workers: pesticide exposure, zoonotic disease risk (from livestock contact), musculoskeletal strain, heat exposure, and mechanical injury from farm equipment — a reminder that “occupational health” is not synonymous with “industrial health.”

title: Occupational Health
text:
Industrial Accidents
🟣 MAY KNOW
~85% of industrial accidents are attributed to human causes (carelessness, fatigue, inadequate training) rather than purely environmental/mechanical ones (unsafe machinery, poor lighting) — a finding with direct implications for prevention strategy: engineering fixes alone are insufficient without training, supervision, and safety culture.
Prevention combines both angles: safety engineering (machine guarding, adequate lighting/ventilation) and human-factor measures (training, enforced safety protocols, adequate rest periods to reduce fatigue-related error).

title: Occupational Health
text:
The Factories Act, 1948
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
India’s principal occupational safety legislation, predating the ESI Act by the same year — together they form the two-pillar legal foundation of Indian occupational health (ESI = health insurance and benefits; Factories Act = workplace safety standards and conditions).
Core provisions include mandated standards for:

Health — cleanliness, ventilation, lighting, drinking water, sanitation
Safety — machine guarding, safe means of access, precautions against fire
Welfare — washing facilities, canteens (in larger factories), rest rooms
Working hours and conditions — limits on daily/weekly working hours, overtime, and employment of young persons
